contents.content:
2,536 tentative vacancies. Read that word "tentative" carefully, because SSC means it literally here — the Commission has said outright that the final count depends on scrutiny of documents from the various user departments, and the real number could shift once that process wraps up. What's already clear, though, is the direction: last year's CHSL cycle opened with 3,131 vacancies, so this year's starting figure is already about 19% lower. If you were banking on CHSL being a bigger draw this year than last, that assumption doesn't hold up against the numbers on the notice.

CHSL sits in an interesting spot within the SSC ecosystem — it's the one major exam here that doesn't demand a degree, just a 12th pass, which keeps the applicant pool enormous even as the seat count shrinks. Last cycle pulled in over 11 lakh candidates for Tier-I alone, and there's no reason to expect this year's pool to be meaningfully smaller just because the vacancy count dropped. Fewer seats, similar or bigger crowd — that combination usually means tighter cutoffs, not gentler ones.

This piece goes through the notification section by section, checks the trend against last year and against SSC's other major exams running this season, and then digs into what's genuinely different about this cycle's exam structure and selection rules — because CHSL has more moving parts (post preferences, sliding mechanism, separate cutoffs per post type) than most candidates realise before they've read past the vacancy number.

How CHSL Compares to Other SSC Exams This Season

CHSL, CGL, and MTS all run under the same Commission but target completely different education levels and pay bands, which is worth keeping in mind if you're weighing more than one this cycle.

Recruitment Tentative Vacancies Fee (Gen-OBC / Exempt) Age Limit Selection Stages
SSC CHSL 2026 2,536 ₹100 / ₹0 (Women, SC, ST, PwBD, ESM) 18–27 years (as on 01-08-2026) Tier-I → Tier-II (4 sections, incl. Skill/Typing Test) → Document Verification
SSC CGL 2026 12,256 ₹100 / exempt for reserved categories 18–32 years, varies by post Tier-I (qualifying) → Tier-II → DEST/Computer module → DV
SSC MTS & Havaldar 2026 Not yet announced in the notification ₹100 / exempt for Women, SC, ST, PwBD, ESM MTS: 18–25 years; Havaldar: 18–27 years Single CBE → PET/PST (Havaldar only) → Document Verification
SSC CHSL — previous cycle (2025) 3,131 (tentative at notification) ₹100 / ₹0 (Women, SC, ST, ESM) 18–27 years Tier-I → Tier-II

CGL's vacancy count towers over CHSL's by roughly five times, but CGL demands a Bachelor's degree, so it's not actually competing for the same applicant pool. MTS is the closer cousin in terms of eligibility (10th pass, lower age band), but its final vacancy figure wasn't out yet at the time of writing — worth tracking separately if you're a 12th-pass candidate deciding where to spread your effort this season.

The Notification, Field by Field

Important Dates

Online Application Window 7 September 2026 to 7 October 2026 (23:00 hrs)
Fee Payment Last Date 8 October 2026 (23:00 hrs)
Application Correction Window 14 to 16 October 2026 (23:00 hrs)
Tier-I Exam Date To be notified later — not fixed at the time of this notice
Tier-II Exam Date To be notified later
Admit Card Made available roughly 2–3 days before each exam stage
Result Not announced — no date given for either Tier's result yet

Application Fee

  • Standard fee: ₹100/-
  • Fully exempt: Women candidates, SC, ST, PwBD, and Ex-Servicemen (ESM) eligible for reservation.
  • Payment modes: BHIM UPI, Net Banking, Visa, MasterCard, Maestro, RuPay Debit Cards.
  • Fee once paid is non-refundable and can't be adjusted against any other SSC exam.

Age Limit (as on 1 August 2026)

  • 18 to 27 years — candidates born between 2 August 1999 and 1 August 2008 qualify.

Age Relaxation

Category Relaxation Beyond Upper Limit
SC/ST 5 years
OBC 3 years
PwBD 10 years
PwBD (OBC) 13 years
PwBD (SC/ST) 15 years
Ex-Servicemen 3 years after deducting military service rendered
Defence personnel disabled in operations 3 years (8 years if SC/ST)
Central Govt civilian employees, 3+ years service Up to 40 years of age (45 if SC/ST)
Widows/Divorced/Judicially Separated Women (not remarried) Up to 35 years of age (40 if SC/ST)

One detail that trips up a fair number of applicants: age relaxation does not extend to sons, daughters, or dependents of Ex-Servicemen — only the Ex-Serviceman themselves qualifies for that category.

Total Vacancy: 2,536 (Tentative)

SSC is explicit that this figure isn't final — it's subject to change once vacancy details are confirmed and scrutinised by the various indenting Ministries and Departments. Updated post-wise and category-wise numbers get published later on the Commission's "Tentative Vacancy" section. Also worth flagging: the Commission does not collect or publish state-wise or zone-wise vacancy splits for this exam at all — if you need that level of detail, you're expected to approach the specific User Department directly rather than SSC.

Pay Scale by Post

Post Pay Level Pay Range
Lower Division Clerk (LDC) / Junior Secretariat Assistant (JSA) Level 2 ₹19,900 – ₹63,200
Data Entry Operator (DEO) Level 4 / Level 5 ₹25,500 – ₹81,100 (Level 4); ₹29,200 – ₹92,300 (Level 5)
Data Entry Operator, Grade 'A' Level 4 ₹25,500 – ₹81,100

Eligibility

  • LDC/JSA and DEO/DEO Grade 'A' (general): 12th Standard pass or equivalent from a recognised Board or University.
  • DEO/DEO Grade 'A' in the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution, SSC itself, and the Ministry of Culture: 12th Standard pass specifically in the Science stream, with Mathematics as a subject.
  • Candidates still awaiting their 12th result can apply, but must actually hold the qualification by the cut-off date, 7 October 2026 — a result "under process" by that date doesn't count; it must be formally declared.

Reservation & Category Certification

SSC itself doesn't decide vacancy splits across SC, ST, OBC, EWS, ESM, and PwBD categories — that responsibility sits with the individual indenting Ministries and Departments. What SSC does enforce is the certification process: candidates claiming a reserved category or age relaxation must produce the correct format of certificate when the concerned department asks for it during Document Verification, or the claim gets rejected outright. OBC candidates specifically need to confirm they don't fall under the creamy layer as of the application closing date, and EWS applicants need an Income & Asset certificate valid for the 2026-27 financial year based on 2025-26 income.

Selection Process

  1. Tier-I — Computer Based Examination, screening stage.
  2. Tier-II — Computer Based Examination in two sessions on the same day, including a mandatory Skill/Typing Test.
  3. Document Verification — conducted by the User Departments after the final result.

Tier-I Exam Pattern

Section Questions Marks
English Language (Basic Knowledge) 25 50
General Intelligence 25 50
Quantitative Aptitude (Basic Arithmetic) 25 50
General Awareness 25 50
Total 100 200

Duration is 60 minutes total, with a 15-minute sectional timer for each part. Negative marking is 0.50 per wrong answer.

Tier-II Exam Pattern

Session Section Questions Marks Duration
Session-I Section-I: Mathematical Abilities + Reasoning & General Intelligence 60 180 1 hour
Section-II: English Language & Comprehension + General Awareness 60 180 1 hour
Session-I (contd.) Section-III: Computer Knowledge Test (qualifying only) 15 45 15 minutes
Session-II Section-IV: Skill Test (DEO posts) or Typing Test (LDC/JSA) — qualifying only — — 10–15 minutes

Negative marking in Tier-II is 1 mark per wrong answer in Sections I, II, and III. Section III and IV don't count toward your score directly — they're mandatory to clear, but your actual merit rank comes only from Sections I and II combined. Skipping or failing the Skill/Typing Test disqualifies you regardless of how well you scored elsewhere.

Skill/Typing Test Standards

  • DEO in the specified departments (higher-speed track): 15,000 key depressions per hour.
  • DEO in other departments: 8,000 key depressions per hour.
  • LDC/JSA Typing Test: 35 words per minute in English, or 30 words per minute in Hindi (your choice, locked in at application time and non-changeable later). Hindi-medium typists must use Mangal font specifically — any other font results in automatic disqualification on this test.

Minimum Qualifying Marks

  • UR: 30%
  • OBC/EWS: 25%
  • All other categories: 20%

These thresholds apply to Tier-I and to Sections I, II, and III of Tier-II. Separate category-wise cutoffs also apply across the three post types (LDC/JSA, DEO in specified departments, DEO elsewhere) — clearing the cutoff for one post type doesn't automatically qualify you for another.

Post Preference & Final Allotment

Before the final result, candidates must submit post and department preferences online. Miss this step, and you're out of consideration entirely for that result round, no matter how well you scored. Once submitted, preferences are locked — final and irreversible, no exceptions. Allotment follows a "sliding mechanism" combined with merit-cum-preference, and once you're allotted a post, you can't get it changed later if you fail to meet post-specific physical, medical, or educational standards for that particular role — your candidature simply gets rejected rather than reassigned.

Exam Centres

You select three centres, in priority order, from within a single SSC region (the notification lists nine regions covering the whole country, each tied to specific states and cities). No requests for centre changes are entertained later at any stage. SSC also reserves the right to add, remove, or reassign centres if needed, so treat your chosen centres as a strong preference rather than a guarantee.

How to Apply

  1. Complete One-Time Registration (OTR) on the new SSC website, ssc.gov.in, or via the mySSC mobile app — old OTR accounts from the earlier ssc.nic.in site don't carry over.
  2. Opt for Aadhaar-based authentication if possible; it protects you from rejection over minor photo or signature formatting issues later.
  3. Fill in the application form with your personal and educational details.
  4. Capture your photograph live through the application module itself — pre-existing photos aren't accepted and lead to rejection.
  5. Upload your signature as a JPEG between 10–20 KB, sized roughly 6.0 cm by 2.0 cm.
  6. Pay the fee (if applicable) and submit before the deadline.

Document Verification & Required Certificates

  • Matriculation/Secondary Certificate and your qualifying Educational Certificate.
  • Caste/Category certificate, if claiming a reserved category.
  • PwBD certificate in the prescribed format, if applicable.
  • For Ex-Servicemen: the prescribed undertaking, and discharge certificate if already discharged from service.
  • No Objection Certificate, if you're already employed in a Government organisation.
  • Name-change documentation (marriage, divorce, or other legal name change), where applicable.

Other Notable Provisions

  • Selected candidates serve a 2-year probation period before confirmation to the post.
  • Every post under this exam carries All India Service Liability — you can be posted anywhere in the country.
  • Ties in Tier-II scores are resolved first by Section-I marks, then Tier-I marks, then by date of birth (older candidates ranked higher).
  • Compensatory time and scribe facilities are available for eligible PwBD candidates, with detailed procedures for registering an own scribe through OTR and Aadhaar authentication.
  • The Commission runs a detailed post-exam integrity review — log analysis, biometric checks, CCTV footage — and malpractice during any stage carries debarment penalties ranging from 1 year for minor infractions up to 7 years for serious offences like impersonation or hacking exam systems.
  • Marriage-related disqualification: candidates who are, or who marry, someone with a living spouse aren't eligible for appointment, barring specific exemptions.

Important Links

Apply Online / OTR Registration ssc.gov.in candidate portal
Login (existing OTR holders) ssc.gov.in login page
Detailed Official Notification Available on ssc.gov.in under Notice Boards
Official Website ssc.gov.in
Toll-Free Helpline 1800 309 3063

What the Falling Vacancy Count Actually Means for You

Going from 3,131 to 2,536 tentative seats is a real cut, not a rounding difference — about 19% fewer opportunities than last cycle, at a time when the applicant pool is unlikely to shrink by anywhere near that much. Last year's Tier-I alone drew over 11 lakh candidates for those 3,131 seats; this year's ratio of applicants to seats is almost certainly going to be worse, not better. If your prep has been sitting at "good enough for last year's cutoff," it's worth pushing that bar higher rather than assuming the same score gets you through this time.

Prep Strategy — Tier-II Deserves Way More Attention Than Most Candidates Give It

Most CHSL prep energy goes into Tier-I because it's the first hurdle, but Tier-II is genuinely where this exam gets decided — your merit rank comes entirely from Tier-II Sections I and II, and Tier-I only gets you into the room. Section-I splits evenly between Mathematical Abilities and Reasoning, both timed independently within the hour, so practising under that exact 30-minutes-each split matters more than open-ended full-length mocks. Section-II gives English Language and Comprehension 40 of the 60 marks in that half, so if your English is your weaker subject, this is the section quietly deciding your final rank more than General Awareness ever will. The typing and skill test stages are qualifying only, but "qualifying only" doesn't mean "low stakes" — fail it, and your Tier-II score becomes irrelevant no matter how high it was. If you're eyeing an LDC/JSA post and haven't touched a typing test in months, get back into regular practice now rather than a week before the exam; hitting 35 wpm cleanly under exam pressure is a different skill than casual typing speed.

Should You Apply — And Which Post?

If your English and Maths are both reasonably strong and you're comfortable clearing a typing speed requirement, CHSL remains one of the more accessible 12+2-level Central Government exams around, even with this year's smaller vacancy count — the pay bands here (Level 2 to Level 5) genuinely beat most state-level clerical postings. Given the choice between post types, DEO in the higher-speed track pays more but demands the steeper 15,000 key-depressions-per-hour standard, so be honest about your typing speed before ranking that preference above LDC/JSA.

If you're still building your typing speed or your English comprehension needs real work, it might be worth treating this cycle as a serious dry run rather than your make-or-break attempt — since your preferences are locked permanently once submitted, ranking a post you're not actually ready for above one you are is a common, avoidable mistake. Honestly, don't put DEO above LDC/JSA in your preference list just because it pays more, if your typing speed genuinely isn't there yet — a rejected candidature after selection is worse than a lower-paying post you actually keep.

Is the 2,536 vacancy figure final, or could it change?

It's explicitly tentative — SSC has said the final count depends on document scrutiny from user departments, and updated post-wise and category-wise numbers get released later on the Commission's website, not with this initial notice.

How does this year's vacancy count compare to last year's CHSL cycle?

Last year opened with 3,131 tentative vacancies against this year's 2,536 — a drop of roughly 19%, so expect tougher competition per seat even if the applicant numbers stay flat.

Can I get zone-wise or state-wise vacancy numbers from SSC?

No — the Commission explicitly states it doesn't collect state-wise or zone-wise vacancy data for this exam, so you'd need to approach the specific User Department directly if that level of detail matters to your decision.

What's the real difference between the two DEO eligibility tracks?

DEO posts in the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, SSC itself, and the Ministry of Culture require 12th Science with Maths specifically, while DEO posts elsewhere and LDC/JSA only need a general 12th pass — so a Commerce or Arts-stream 12th pass rules you out of that specific DEO track.

Can I change my post preference after submitting it?

No — once submitted, preferences are treated as final and irreversible under any circumstances, and if you don't submit preferences within the given window at all, you won't be considered for any post regardless of your merit rank.

Does the Skill or Typing Test actually count toward my score?

No, it's qualifying only and doesn't add marks, but it's mandatory — failing it disqualifies you from final selection even if your Tier-II written score was strong enough on its own.

How many times can I correct my application if I make a mistake?

Up to two corrections during the 14–16 October window, with a ₹200 charge for the first correction and ₹500 for the second — after that, no further changes are entertained under any circumstances.

Everything above reflects the CHSL 2026 Notice of Examination as published on 7 September 2026. Vacancy figures are officially tentative and subject to revision, and exam dates for both Tiers are yet to be announced, so it's worth checking ssc.gov.in directly and regularly rather than treating this or any single summary as the final word before you apply.

contents.content:
13,706 posts. That's the number IBPS put out this year for its Regional Rural Bank drive, and it's not a small bump from last year — CRP RRBs-XIV in 2025 had 13,217 seats, so this cycle adds roughly 489 more, a rise of just under 4%. Not dramatic, but in a recruitment this size, even a few hundred extra seats change how competitive individual banks end up being. What makes RRB recruitment different from IBPS Clerk or IBPS PO is that it's really four exams bundled under one notification — Office Assistant, Officer Scale-I, Officer Scale-II (with seven separate specialist streams inside it), and Officer Scale-III. You're not picking one exam. You're picking a track, and the track decides everything from your age eligibility to whether you'll sit an interview at all.

Office Assistant is where most of the volume sits — 8,183 of the 13,706 posts, or almost 60% of the entire drive. Officer Scale-I comes next at 4,256. The Scale-II and Scale-III postings are comparatively tiny (1,047 and 220), and several of those Scale-II specialist roles — Treasury Manager at 18 seats, Marketing Officer at 16 — are genuinely narrow doors that only make sense if your degree already points that way. If you're a general graduate weighing your odds, Office Assistant and Officer Scale-I are where the real competition, and the real opportunity, both live.

This piece goes through the entire notification field by field, compares it against IBPS Clerk, IBPS PO, and SBI Clerk running in the same season, and then gets into what actually matters for your prep — because there isn't much point rehashing dates you can already read on the notice itself.

How RRB 2026 Stacks Up Against Other Bank Exams This Season

Same recruiter, mostly the same syllabus family, but very different vacancy sizes and eligibility rules depending on which post you're comparing. Here's where things stand across the four big drives running right now.

Recruitment Total Posts Fee (Gen/Reserved) Age Limit Selection Stages
IBPS RRB 15th (CRP RRBs-XV) 2026 13,706 ₹850 / ₹175 18–28 (Office Asst.) up to 21–40 (Scale-III), post-wise Prelims → Mains → Interview (Officer cadres only) → DV & Medical
IBPS Clerk (CSA) CRP-XVI 2026 11,403 ₹850 / ₹175 20–28 years Prelims → Mains → Local Language Test → DV
IBPS PO (CRP PO/MT-XVI) 2026 7,365 (revised from 6,715) ₹850 / ₹175 20–30 years Prelims → Mains → Interview
SBI Clerk (Junior Associate) 2026 9,766 (7,680 regular + 2,086 backlog) ₹750 / Nil for SC-ST-PwBD-ESM 20–28 years Prelims → Mains → Local Language Test
IBPS RRB 14th (CRP RRBs-XIV) — previous cycle, 2025 13,217 ₹850 / ₹175 18–28 to 21–40, post-wise Prelims → Mains → Interview (Officers)

RRB's Office Assistant track is the only one of these that opens up at 18, which matters if you finished college early and don't want to wait around. IBPS PO, meanwhile, is genuinely the toughest door in raw numbers — 7,365 seats against RRB's combined officer count of roughly 5,523 — but PO carries a compulsory interview for everyone, where RRB's Office Assistant skips it entirely. If your interview skills are shaky, that alone might tilt your priority toward the clerk-side posts across all three of these drives rather than PO.

The Notification, Field by Field

Here's the full breakdown, straight from the notice — nothing trimmed, nothing summarised into vagueness.

Important Dates

Online Application Start 1 September 2026
Online Application Last Date 21 September 2026
Fee Payment Last Date 21 September 2026
Pre-Exam Training (PET) November 2026
Preliminary Exam Date Not announced — the notification lists this as "Notify Later"
Preliminary Admit Card Before the exam; exact date not out
Preliminary Result Not announced yet
Main Exam Date Not specified in the notice as of now

Worth flagging separately: unlike some other IBPS drives this year, there's no correction-window date published on this particular notice — so if you spot an error after submitting, keep checking ibps.in directly rather than assuming a fixed edit window will show up automatically.

Application Fee

  • General, OBC, EWS: ₹850/-
  • SC, ST, PH (PwBD): ₹175/-
  • Payment modes: Debit Card, Credit Card, Internet Banking, IMPS, Cash Card/Mobile Wallet.

Age Limit (as on 1 September 2026) — Post-Wise

Post Age Limit
Office Assistant (Multipurpose) 18–28 years
Officer Scale-I (Assistant Manager) 18–30 years
Officer Scale-II (Manager) 21–32 years
Officer Scale-III (Senior Manager) 21–40 years

Age relaxation applies on top of these limits as per IBPS RRB rules — the standard bands (5 years SC/ST, 3 years OBC non-creamy layer, 10 years PwBD, defence-service relaxation for Ex-servicemen) apply, though the exact figures for this specific cycle sit in the detailed notification rather than the short notice.

Total Vacancy: 13,706 Posts

Post Name No. of Posts
Office Assistant (Multipurpose) 8,183
Officer Scale-I (Assistant Manager) 4,256
Officer Scale-II (General Banking Officer) 666
Officer Scale-II (Information Technology Officer) 182
Officer Scale-II (Chartered Accountant) 81
Officer Scale-II (Law Officer) 46
Officer Scale-II (Treasury Manager) 18
Officer Scale-II (Marketing Officer) 16
Officer Scale-II (Agriculture Officer) 38
Officer Scale-III (Senior Manager) 220
Total 13,706

The full state-wise and category-wise breakup (across the 28 participating RRBs) runs into several pages and is published separately in the detailed notification annexure on ibps.in — worth pulling up once you've picked your preferred bank or state, since seat counts vary sharply from one RRB to another.

Eligibility

Post Eligibility
Office Assistant (Multipurpose) Graduation in any discipline from a recognised university/institute. Proficiency in the local language of the RRB applied to. Working knowledge of computers is desirable, not compulsory.
Officer Scale-I (Assistant Manager) Graduation in any discipline. Preference given to Agriculture, Horticulture, Forestry, Animal Husbandry, Veterinary Science, Agricultural Engineering, Pisciculture, Agricultural Marketing & Cooperation, IT, Management, Law, Economics, or Accountancy degrees. Local language proficiency required.
Officer Scale-II (General Banking Officer) Graduation with a minimum 50% marks, plus 2 years' experience as an officer in a bank or financial institution.
Officer Scale-II (IT) Degree in Electronics/Communications/Computer Science/IT with 50% marks; certificates in ASP, PHP, C++, Java, VB, VC, OCP etc. desirable; 1 year relevant experience.
Officer Scale-II (CA) Passed CA from ICAI, plus 1 year experience as a Chartered Accountant.
Officer Scale-II (Law) Law degree with minimum 50% aggregate; 2 years as an advocate or Law Officer in a bank/financial institution.
Officer Scale-II (Treasury Manager) CA or MBA in Finance, plus 1 year relevant experience.
Officer Scale-II (Marketing Officer) MBA in Marketing, plus 1 year relevant experience.
Officer Scale-II (Agriculture Officer) Graduation in Agriculture/Horticulture/Dairy/Animal Science/Veterinary Science/Engineering/Pisciculture, plus 2 years relevant experience.
Officer Scale-III (Senior Manager) Bachelor's degree with minimum 50% aggregate, preference for banking/finance-adjacent degrees, and a minimum 5 years' experience as an officer in a bank or financial institution.

Notice the pattern here — Office Assistant and Officer Scale-I are open to any fresh graduate, but everything from Scale-II onward wants prior work experience. That single detail rules out most fresher applicants automatically, whether or not they realise it while filling the form.

Selection Process

  1. Preliminary Exam — applies to all posts, qualifying stage.
  2. Main Exam — for Officer Scale-I and Office Assistant. Scale-II and III sit a single combined exam instead of a separate prelims/mains split.
  3. Interview — Officer Scale-I, II, and III only. Office Assistant has none.
  4. Document Verification & Medical Examination.

This is the detail that surprises Office Assistant aspirants who've also applied for Officer Scale-I in parallel — one post drops them straight into allotment after Mains, the other adds a full interview round on top. Worth planning your prep calendar around that difference rather than treating both tracks identically.

Exam Pattern — Office Assistant & Officer Scale-I

Stage Section Questions Marks Duration
Prelims Reasoning 40 40 45 minutes total
Numerical Ability 40 40
Mains Reasoning 40 50 120 minutes total
Numerical Ability 40 50
General Awareness 40 40
English or Hindi Language 40 40
Computer Knowledge 40 20

Negative marking is 0.25 per wrong answer at both stages. Officer Scale-II and III sit a single online exam instead — the exact section-wise split for this specific CRP RRBs-XV cycle wasn't detailed in the short notice, so go by "as notified" until the full annexure is out closer to the exam date.

Salary and Pay Scale

Post Starting Basic Pay Approx. Gross/In-Hand (Monthly)
Office Assistant (Multipurpose) ₹24,050 Roughly ₹33,000–40,000, city-dependent
Officer Scale-I ₹48,480 Roughly ₹57,000–74,000
Officer Scale-II ₹64,820 Roughly ₹75,000+
Officer Scale-III ₹85,920 Roughly ₹90,000+

These figures move with Dearness Allowance, House Rent Allowance, and posting location — a metro branch pushes the number up, a rural branch pulls it down. Treat them as a reasonable estimate rather than a fixed payslip.

How to Apply

Applications for Office Assistant and for the Officer cadres go through two separate registration links on ibps.in, not one shared form — worth double-checking you're on the correct portal before you start filling anything in. Beyond that, it's the usual sequence: register with a working phone number and email, log back in to complete personal, educational, and category details, upload photo and signature in the specified size, and pay the fee online. One rule that trips people up every cycle — you're allowed to apply for Office Assistant and for one Officer post at the same time, but you cannot apply across multiple Officer scales. Pick Scale-I, II, or III; you don't get all three.

Important Links

Apply Online (Office Assistant) ibpsreg.ibps.in — registration portal (rrboaxvaug26)
Apply Online (Officer Scale I/II/III) ibpsreg.ibps.in — registration portal (rrbxvaug26)
Detailed Official Notification PDF Available on ibps.in under CRP RRBs-XV
Syllabus / Exam Pattern PDF Available on ibps.in under CRP RRBs-XV
Official Website ibps.in

Prep Strategy — What Actually Helps Right Now

If you're going for Office Assistant or Officer Scale-I, Prelims is 80 marks split evenly between Reasoning and Numerical Ability, and both run on the same 45-minute clock — no section-wise time limit here unlike some newer bank exams, which honestly works in your favour if one section is your weaker side. Use that flexibility. Don't burn 30 minutes on Reasoning puzzles and leave Numerical Ability rushed. Mains is where the real gap between Office Assistant and Officer Scale-I opens up. Both sit the same five sections, but Officer Scale-I candidates also need to think ahead to the interview — General Awareness questions there often circle back during the interview itself, so treat that section as long-term prep, not a two-week cram. Computer Knowledge is worth only 20 marks out of 200, low-effort and high-return if you just cover the basics once, properly, rather than obsessing over it.

One thing that's easy to underrate: local language proficiency is a listed requirement for both Office Assistant and Officer Scale-I, but unlike IBPS Clerk or SBI Clerk, there's no separate Local Language Test mentioned after Mains in this notice — which suggests it's verified at the document stage instead. If your reading and writing in the relevant state's language isn't strong, that's still worth fixing before you get to document verification, not after.

Should You Apply — And Which Track?

If you're a fresh graduate without work experience, Office Assistant and Officer Scale-I are realistically your only two options here — everything from Scale-II onward asks for 1 to 5 years in banking, finance, or a specific professional qualification. Between those two, it comes down to how comfortable you are with an interview. Officer Scale-I pays significantly more and starts your career on the officer track, but you'll need to carry that Mains performance through a face-to-face round afterward. Office Assistant skips that entirely — Mains alone decides your fate.

If you already work in banking or hold a CA, law, or MBA-Finance qualification, the Scale-II specialist posts are worth a serious look precisely because so few people qualify for them. Fewer eligible applicants usually means a gentler cutoff, even with a smaller seat count. Don't dismiss an 18-seat category just because the number looks small — the applicant pool shrinks even faster than the vacancy count does.

How many total vacancies does IBPS RRB 15th 2026 actually have, and where's most of it?

13,706 posts in total, and nearly 60% of that — 8,183 seats — sits in the Office Assistant category alone.

Can I apply for Office Assistant and an Officer post together?

Yes, that combination is allowed, but you can only pick one of the three Officer scales alongside it — not more than one officer cadre in the same cycle.

Does Office Assistant have an interview like the Officer posts do?

No. Interview applies only to Officer Scale-I, II, and III. Office Assistant selection is based on the Main Exam alone, which is a real relief if interviews aren't your strength.

Is this year's vacancy count actually bigger than last year's, or does it just sound that way?

It is bigger, just not by much — 13,706 against 13,217 in the CRP RRBs-XIV cycle last year, which works out to under a 4% rise.

Why do some Officer Scale-II posts need work experience while Office Assistant doesn't?

Scale-II and III are lateral-entry-style specialist and managerial roles, so IBPS expects 1 to 5 years of relevant experience depending on the post — Office Assistant and Scale-I, by contrast, are entry-level and open to any fresh graduate.

What's the actual pay difference between Office Assistant and Officer Scale-I?

Office Assistant starts at a basic of ₹24,050, while Officer Scale-I starts at ₹48,480 — roughly double, before allowances are even added in.

Has the exam date for Prelims been announced yet?

Not as of this notification — it's still listed as "Notify Later," so keep checking ibps.in rather than relying on any tentative date floating around on forums or social media.

Numbers and dates here are as published in the short notice as of this writing — IBPS has a track record of revising vacancy counts, exam dates, and even eligibility fine print through corrigenda later in the cycle. Before you act on anything above, it's worth pulling up the detailed notification PDF on ibps.in yourself and checking it against your own category and post.

How to Prepare for This Specific Paper

The written exam's structure tells you exactly where to put your hours. General Knowledge of Uttarakhand alone carries 40 of the 100 marks — the same weight as national GK & General Studies combined. Don't treat this as a minor regional add-on. State-specific history, geography, culture, government schemes, and current affairs deserve as much prep time as the national GK section, arguably more, since fewer aspirants outside Uttarakhand bother mastering it deeply, which means it's exactly where scores separate.

With negative marking at 0.25 per wrong answer and a 45%/35% qualifying bar, guessing recklessly isn't smart here. Attempt what you're reasonably confident about; skip pure guesses on questions where you have no real basis for an answer, since the penalty adds up over 100 questions.

Don't underestimate the typing test just because it's qualifying-only. A 4,000 KDPH Hindi typing requirement isn't trivial if you've never practiced on a proper keyboard layout for Devanagari script. Start practicing now, not after your written exam result — there won't be much runway between the two stages, going by how these UKSSSC cycles have run before.

If you're eyeing a post with additional requirements — the BRIDCUL Pravar Sahayak's experience clause, or the Transport Department's employment exchange registration — get that paperwork sorted well ahead of the application window. These aren't things you can arrange in the final week.

Should You Apply? A Straightforward Read

If you're a 12th-pass candidate with decent Hindi typing speed and solid Uttarakhand-specific GK, this cycle is genuinely worth your shot — the eligibility bar being lower than earlier cycles works in your favour, not against it.

If you're a graduate who's been waiting for a "graduate-only" UKSSSC drive to reduce competition, this isn't that exam. Everyone from 12th-pass candidates upward can apply, so don't expect your degree to thin the field.

If you're specifically after the BRIDCUL Pravar Sahayak post or another experience-based role in this list, only apply if you genuinely meet the multi-year experience clause — these aren't fresher-friendly postings despite sitting in the same notification.

Honestly, if you're chasing a specific department for personal reasons — wanting to work near home, say — check that department's exact vacancy count first. What's the last date to apply, and is fee payment on a separate schedule?

Both close on 07 October 2026 — application submission and fee payment share the same deadline this time, so don't leave the fee for later.

553 in total, and Registration Clerk under the Stamp & Registration Department leads with 55 posts on its own — the single largest allocation in this notification.

Yes, from 12 to 14 October 2026 — a short three-day window after the application closes, so it's worth reviewing your form carefully before submission rather than relying on this to fix everything.

No. This cycle's baseline qualification is Intermediate (Class 12), a step down from the Bachelor's degree requirement UKSSSC used for its comparable Junior Assistant drive back in 2019-20.

No, it's purely qualifying. Your final merit is decided entirely by written exam marks, so a strong written score matters far more than typing speed beyond the minimum threshold.

The older candidate gets ranked higher first; if birth dates also match exactly, alphabetical order of name settles it — a tie-break rule worth knowing if you're right at a cutoff.

contents.content:
55 posts. That's genuinely small next to the bank and railway drives flooding the job market this season, and honestly, that's the whole story with IIT non-teaching recruitment — it's never a mass-hiring exercise. IIT (BHU) has bundled five cadres into a single advertisement this time: Administrative, Technical, Library, Engineering, and Rajbhasha (Hindi translation). Most cycles at IIT BHU come out as separate, narrower notices for just one or two of these cadres. Combining them into one advertisement this year probably makes the HR side's life easier, but for an applicant it also means the eligibility bar swings wildly from post to post within the same notification — a Junior Technician needs a plain Bachelor's degree, while an Assistant Engineer needs five years of prior experience at a specific pay level just to be considered.

Of the 55 seats, Junior Superintendent alone takes 21 — more than a third of the entire drive — and it's also one of only two posts here (the other being Assistant Engineer) that demands real post-qualification experience rather than just a degree. If you're a fresh graduate with zero work history, your actual playing field shrinks to Junior Technician (Groups I–V, 26 seats combined) and Junior Library Assistant (2 seats). Everything else wants years on the job already.

This piece walks through the notification field by field, checks it against how IIT BHU and its sister institutes have run similar drives recently, and then gets into what's worth doing differently depending on which post you're eyeing.

How This Compares to Other IIT Non-Teaching Drives Running This Season

IITs don't run one shared national exam like IBPS or SSC does — each institute recruits on its own calendar, which makes side-by-side comparison a bit messier, but the pattern across institutes is still worth seeing.

IIT Kanpur's 80-post drive is the biggest of this batch, but it also spans Group A officer-level posts (Deputy Registrar, Superintending Engineer) that need a master's degree and years of seniority — not something a fresh graduate is touching. IIT BHU's notification, by contrast, tops out at Assistant Engineer, so it's a friendlier document for someone earlier in their career, even with the smaller headline number.

On the "how many posts have opened here before" question — IIT BHU doesn't run one consolidated annual non-teaching exam the way IBPS or SSC does. It splits Administrative, Technical, and Library cadres across separate advertisements in different years, so there's no clean apples-to-apples "last year's total" to quote. The closest comparable notice is the Technical & Library advertisement from December 2023, which covered Junior Technician (Groups I–III only, not V groups like this cycle) plus two library posts — around 49 seats combined. The notification doesn't spell out which stages apply to which post — a technical Junior Technician role is unlikely to involve a Group Discussion the way Junior Superintendent might, going by how IIT BHU has structured similar drives before. Mere eligibility doesn't guarantee a call for any of these stages either; the Institute explicitly reserves the right to apply "more stringent criteria" for shortlisting than what's published, and to prefer candidates with higher qualifications or merit.

How to Apply

Applications go entirely through the SAMARTH portal at iitbhunt.samarth.edu.in — no other submission method is accepted. But the online form isn't the end of it. After submitting, you're required to print the completed application, attach self-attested photocopies of your documents and an experience certificate (in the prescribed Annexure-A format, if claiming experience), and send the whole packet by Speed Post to the Registrar, IIT (BHU), Varanasi – 221005, within seven days of the application deadline. If your employer needs to forward it (relevant for anyone already in government service), that has to happen through proper channel within the same window, or the application risks not being considered at all. Skip that step and the online submission alone won't carry you through — it's a two-part process, not one.

Required Documents & Other Notes

  • SC/ST/OBC candidates need caste certificates in the prescribed GoI format; OBC applicants specifically need a non-creamy-layer certificate no older than six months.
  • Candidates already working in Government/Semi-Government organisations, Autonomous Bodies, or Educational Institutions must upload a No Objection Certificate and Vigilance Clearance with their application — failing that, they'll need to produce both at the interview stage instead.
  • Experience claims need a certificate in the Annexure-A format signed by the competent authority of the previous employer.
  • The Institute reserves the right to increase, decrease, or entirely cancel vacancies for any post without giving a reason — worth remembering before you get too attached to any specific seat count.
  • Selected candidates may be appointed on contract instead of a regular post, at the Institute's discretion, depending on performance in the selection process.

Prep Strategy — Post by Post, Not One-Size-Fits-All

There's no single syllabus running across these ten posts, which is exactly why a generic "study hard" plan falls apart here. If you're going for Junior Technician in any of the five groups, your core qualification is already the filter — the written test, from how IIT BHU has run these before, tends to lean on core-branch technical knowledge from your engineering syllabus rather than general aptitude, so dust off your third and fourth-year subject notes rather than reasoning-and-quant prep books meant for bank exams. Junior Superintendent is a different animal entirely — it's an administrative post, and going by the stages listed (Group Discussion, Presentation, Interview), general awareness, office procedure, and communication skills probably matter more than technical depth. If you've got the 3 or 8 years of experience this post demands, brushing up on general financial and HR procedures relevant to a government/PSU office is a better use of your remaining weeks than pure subject revision.

For Assistant Engineer and Junior Engineer, the experience bar does most of the filtering before the exam even starts — with only 2 and 3 seats respectively, this isn't a volume game, and your actual technical depth from years on the job will matter more than last-minute cramming.

Should You Apply — And to Which Post?

If you're a fresh graduate with no work experience, Junior Technician and Junior Library Assistant are genuinely your only realistic options in this notification — everything else demands years of prior service. Among the five Junior Technician groups, Group-II (Mechanical/Metallurgical/Ceramic/Materials Science) has the most seats at 11, so it's statistically your best shot if your branch fits, though "most seats" doesn't always mean "easiest cutoff" once you account for how many people in that branch are also applying.

If you already have several years in a government office, PSU, or research organisation, Junior Superintendent is worth serious consideration — 21 seats is a genuinely large opening for a Level 6 administrative post at an IIT, and that scale doesn't come around often. Honestly, if you don't clear the specific experience threshold (3 years at Level 5, or 8 years at Level 3), don't waste the ₹500 fee — the eligibility here isn't the kind of thing that gets relaxed at the shortlisting stage.

How many total posts are up for grabs, and which one has the most seats?

55 posts across five cadres, and Junior Superintendent alone accounts for 21 of them — well over a third of the entire notification.

Can I edit my application after submitting it if I make a mistake?

No — the notification is explicit that no change, correction, or modification is allowed once the form is submitted, under any circumstances, so it's worth reviewing every field twice before you hit submit.

Is submitting the online form on SAMARTH enough, or is there more to it?

There's more — you also need to post a signed printout of your application along with self-attested documents to the Registrar by Speed Post within seven days of the deadline, or your candidature could be dropped from further consideration.

Do SC/ST/PwBD candidates pay a different fee, or none at all?

None at all — SC, ST, PwBD (Divyangjan), and all-female candidates are fully exempt from the fee for every post here, whether it's a Group B post at ₹500 or a Group C post at ₹250 for everyone else.

Is this recruitment bigger or smaller than IIT BHU's last comparable drive?

Based on available records, the closest earlier comparable notice (technical and library cadre, December 2023) covered around 49 posts, though it spanned a narrower set of cadres than this year's 55 — so a direct percentage comparison isn't really reliable here.

What's actually different between Junior Technician and Junior Superintendent, besides the subject matter?

Junior Technician needs zero prior work experience and pays at Level 3, while Junior Superintendent demands 3 to 8 years of relevant government or PSU experience and pays at the considerably higher Level 6 — they're not really competing pools of candidates.

If I already work in a government job, is there anything extra I need to submit?

Yes — you'll need a No Objection Certificate and Vigilance Clearance from your current employer uploaded with your application, or you'll have to produce both later at the interview stage instead.

Everything above reflects Advertisement No. 03/2026-27 as published. IIT (BHU) has explicitly reserved the right to increase, reduce, or withdraw any of these posts, and vacancy numbers or eligibility fine print can shift through a corrigendum later in the cycle — so before you spend the application fee, it's worth pulling up the notification yourself on iitbhu.ac.in and checking it against your own post and category.

contents.content:
India Post has opened 23,757 Gramin Dak Sevak (GDS) posts under the Online Engagement Schedule-II, July-2026 cycle, and honestly, the number itself tells a story if you compare it against recent cycles. It's lower than the Schedule-I, January 2026 round, which had brought in 28,740 vacancies. That's a drop of roughly 17%, based on the figures published in that earlier notification. But it's still higher than the February-March 2025 cycle, which closed at 21,413 posts. So the trend isn't a straight line up or down — it's more of a wave, tied to how many BPM/ABPM/GDS positions actually fall vacant across circles each cycle.

What does that mean for you as an applicant? Competition will vary sharply by category and by circle, not uniformly. General category alone accounts for 10,640 of the 23,757 posts — that's close to 45% of the total pie. OBC gets 4,433, SC 3,082, ST 2,773, and EWS 2,160. If you fall in General or EWS, expect the cutoff percentages to stay high, because these categories typically draw the largest applicant pools relative to seats. SC and ST candidates, meanwhile, historically see comparatively lower merit cutoffs in GDS recruitment, simply because fewer candidates compete within those reserved pools per seat.

Circle-wise, the spread is uneven too. North Eastern circle tops the list with 2,504 posts, followed by Maharashtra (2,431), Tamil Nadu (2,118), and West Bengal (1,762). Uttar Pradesh, which usually posts big numbers in GDS cycles, has 1,691 seats this time — noticeably lower than some past cycles. If you're from a smaller circle like Delhi (just 16 posts) or Punjab (122), don't expect quick assured entries; the math simply isn't in your favour there. Candidates who know the local language for a circle with more seats but are willing to relocate might genuinely improve their odds, since local language knowledge is a hard eligibility filter and not everyone can meet it.

Note: All figures above come directly from the official notification and its annexures. Circle allocations, category splits, and cutoffs can be revised by India Post at any stage, so always cross-check the live notification on indiapostgdsonline.gov.in before finalising your decision to apply.

GDS vs Other Class-10 Level Government Exams: A Quick Comparison

GDS often gets compared to Railway Group D and SSC CHSL because all three sit at roughly the same educational entry point. But the similarities end there — the selection mechanics are completely different, and that difference actually matters more than most applicants realise when they're deciding where to put their energy.

Parameter India Post GDS (Sch-II, July 2026) RRB Group D (CEN 09/2025) SSC CHSL 2026
Total Vacancies 23,757 22,195 ~2,536 (tentative)

Application Fee (General/OBC) ₹100 ₹500 (partly refundable on CBT appearance) ₹100
Fee for SC/ST/PWD/Women Nil ₹250 Nil
Written Exam? No — merit purely on Class 10 marks Yes — CBT with negative marking Yes — Tier I & Tier II CBT

Notice the fee gap between GDS and Group D. That ₹500 fee for Group D isn't trivial for a fresher, and combined with the CBT prep timeline, it's a bigger commitment overall. GDS, on the other hand, needs zero preparation for a written test — your Class 10 marksheet has already decided most of your fate. That's precisely why lakhs of candidates who never plan to work as a postal employee long-term still apply for GDS: it costs little, takes an afternoon to fill, and doesn't eat into months of study time meant for a bigger exam like Group D or CHSL.

Preparation Strategy That Actually Fits This Recruitment

Here's the thing most GDS guides get wrong: they tell you to "study hard," which makes zero sense for an exam that doesn't exist. There's no written test here. Your entire game is your Class 10 percentage, so the real prep work happens before you even open the application form.

Start by recalculating your Class 10 percentage exactly the way India Post does it — using marks from all subjects, not just the ones you scored well in. Boards that give grades instead of marks (CBSE, for instance, in certain years) require a specific conversion method, and getting this wrong is one of the most common reasons candidates end up ranked lower than they expected. Don't eyeball it; redo the calculation on paper using the formula mentioned in the notification, subject by subject.

Second, get your documents in order well before 21 September. That means your Class 10 marksheet, local language proof (a separate certificate if your marksheet doesn't explicitly show the language subject), category certificate if applicable, and PwBD certificate where relevant. A shockingly large number of GDS applications get rejected at the document verification stage — not because candidates weren't eligible, but because their language proof didn't match circle requirements, or their category certificate had expired.

Third, use the correction window smartly. The 23–24 September window exists precisely because people make errors under form-filling pressure. Circle selection, category, and language declaration are the fields to triple-check — changing your circle after the merit list is out isn't an option.

Lastly, if you're eyeing multiple circles because you know more than one local language, apply strategically rather than emotionally. Pick the circle where your Class 10 percentage would land you comfortably above last cycle's cutoff, not just your hometown by default.

Should You Apply? A Decision Framework

If you scored above 90% in Class 10 and know a high-demand circle's local language, apply without overthinking it — your odds here are genuinely strong, and the zero-exam format means you lose nothing by trying.

If you're a fresher with an average Class 10 score (say, 60-75%) from a low-vacancy circle like Delhi or Punjab, apply anyway but keep expectations realistic. Treat this as a backup, not your primary plan.

If you're deep into RRB Group D or SSC CHSL preparation, there's genuinely no conflict in also applying to GDS — the application takes an hour, costs ₹100 at most, and doesn't touch your exam study time at all.

If you already worked as a GDS in a previous cycle and resigned or were removed for disciplinary reasons, check the specific eligibility clause in the notification regarding past engagement history before applying again this cycle — this detail is easy to miss and can lead to rejection later.

Honestly, if your Class 10 marks were weak and you don't meet the local language requirement for any high-vacancy circle nearby, this particular cycle probably isn't your best shot. Wait for a cycle where your home circle opens more seats, rather than applying somewhere you'd have to relocate with slim odds.

Frequently Asked Questions

What's the last date to apply for GDS 2026?

21 September 2026, that's the cutoff for submitting the form. But don't wait till then — your OTR needs to be done first, and that window shuts on 19 September. Miss the OTR and the rest doesn't matter.

How many total vacancies are there?

23,757, across the board. General takes the biggest chunk at 10,640, then OBC, SC, ST, EWS, and four separate PWD categories fill in the rest.

Is there a written exam?

Nope, none. Your Class 10 marks do all the talking here. Clear the merit cut, get your documents verified, and that's basically it.

What's the application fee?

₹100 if you're General or OBC. If you're SC, ST, PH, or a woman applying under any category, you don't pay anything at all.

What qualification do I need?

A Class 10 pass with Maths and English from a recognised board is non-negotiable. You'll also need to show you've studied the local language for whichever circle you're applying to — skip this and your application won't hold up at verification.

Which circle has the most vacancies this time?

North Eastern circle leads with 2,504 posts. Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu aren't far behind either, at 2,431 and 2,118. If your local language matches one of these, your odds just got a bit better.

Is OTR the same thing as the final application?

They get mixed up a lot, but no. OTR is just you registering yourself in the system. The actual form — where you pick your circle, post office preferences, everything — comes after, starting 2 September 2026.

contents.content:
388 posts, one single notification. The number looks big on paper, but the competition is going to be just as tight, because this drive includes Clerk and Stenographer roles — the kind of "evergreen" categories every graduate in the state keeps half an eye on. The High Court of Himachal Pradesh, Shimla, released Advertisement Notice No. DJ-ADVT./2026 (1) on 5 August 2026, and applications opened on 10 August. The window closes on 10 September 2026, at 11:59 PM. This recruitment is for the District Judiciary establishment, not the High Court's own office staff — the two are separate services, and we'll unpack that distinction later in the FAQ.

Here's an honest starting point: if you're eyeing the Clerk or Stenographer numbers and getting excited about 141 and 79 openings, hold on for a second. A large chunk of these are Contract-mode posts, not Regular ones, so a defined pay scale isn't guaranteed to everyone who clears the test. Below, we've laid out the complete post-wise and category-wise vacancy split, fees, age limits, eligibility, and selection process — table by table — along with a genuine comparison of how similar clerk and Group-D recruitments are shaping up elsewhere in the country right now.

How Big Is This Recruitment, Really — A Comparison With Similar Exams

Raw numbers alone don't tell you much about how good an opportunity actually is. So we lined up this HP High Court drive against three other recruitments running around the same time — Rajasthan's LDC cycle, Rajasthan High Court's Group-D drive, and HP's own Police Constable recruitment from earlier this year.

Recruitment Total Posts Fee (Gen/Reserved) Age Limit Minimum Education Selection Stages
HP High Court Various Post 2026 388 ₹450 / ₹300 18–45 (up to 50, category-wise) 10+2 to Graduation, varies by post Screening/Written, Typing/Stenography or Driving Test (post-specific), Document Verification
RSSB Rajasthan LDC 2026 10,644 ₹600 / ₹400 18–40 12th pass + CET qualifying Written Exam (OMR), Document Verification, Typing Test
Rajasthan High Court Group-D 2025 5,670 Category-wise (approx.) 18–40 10th/12th pass (post-wise) Written Exam, Interview
HP Police Constable 2026 734 ₹600 (all categories) 18–25 (General) 12th pass Written, Physical, Medical

One thing stands out immediately: HP High Court's fee is noticeably lower than most other state-level exams here, and its age limit is quite a bit more relaxed too, especially for reserved-category candidates who get a straight run up to 50. That's a genuinely candidate-friendly notification on paper. That said, a pool like Rajasthan's LDC drive draws candidates from the entire state into one exam, so despite the huge post count, the competition per seat will likely be just as fierce. Selection here is also split by district and category to some extent, which can work in favour of HP domicile candidates specifically.

The Complete Notification, Field By Field

Important Dates

Advertisement Notice Date 5 August 2026
Online Application Start 10 August 2026
Online Application Last Date 10 September 2026 (11:59 PM)
Fee Payment Last Date 10 September 2026 (along with the application)
Exam Date Not announced yet — the notification simply says "Notify Soon"
Admit Card Will be issued before the exam; no exact date given so far
Result To be updated later; no tentative date has been mentioned

Application Fee

  • General category: ₹450/- (GST included)
  • SC / ST / OBC / EWS / PH (HP domicile candidates only): ₹300/- (GST included)
  • Payment must be made online — Debit Card, Credit Card, Net Banking, IMPS, or Mobile Wallet/Cash Card.
  • Once the fee is paid, it will not be refunded under any circumstances.

Age Limit (as reckoned on 1 January 2026)

  • Minimum Age: 18 years
  • Maximum Age (UR/EWS): 45 years
  • Maximum Age (HP's reserved categories — SC/ST/OBC/PH — and HP Government employees): 50 years (with the standard 5-year relaxation built in)
  • Exception: the Court Manager post has its own age band entirely — 25 to 35 years, with no mention of anyone outside that range being considered.

Total Vacancy: 388 Posts — Post-Wise and Category-Wise Breakdown

Post Name Group Total Posts Mode Breakdown Pay Level (Regular)

Clerk Group-C 141 Regular – 84, Contract – 57 Level-03 (₹20,200 – ₹64,000)
Stenographer Grade-III Group-C 79 Regular – 48, Contract – 31 Level-06 (₹25,600 – ₹81,200)

For Contract and Daily Wages posts, pay isn't drawn from a fixed pay-matrix level at all — it's "wages/remuneration as fixed by the Govt. of HP from time to time," which the notification states plainly. Getting a Regular post gets you the pay matrix shown above, but even then, your initial posting could still land in Contract or Daily Wages mode depending on category and merit position.

Eligibility (Educational Qualification and Experience)

Post Qualification / Experience
Court Manager Graduation in any stream plus an MBA from a UGC-recognized institution, along with 3 years' experience in Process Management, IT Systems Management, HR Management, or Financial Management. Knowledge of legal affairs and computers is listed as desirable, not mandatory.
Clerk Graduation degree plus basic computer knowledge (operating Windows/Linux, taking printouts). Typing speed of 30 WPM in English and 25 WPM in Hindi (Kruti Dev-10 font) on computer.
Stenographer Grade-III Graduation degree plus English Stenography at 80 WPM, along with 40 WPM English and 30 WPM Hindi typing (Kruti Dev-10 font). Transcription has to be completed within 5 times the dictation time, and more than 10% mistakes disqualify a candidate.
Driver Matriculation pass plus a valid LMV licence plus at least 3 years of driving experience. Candidates with mechanical knowledge get preference.
Process Server 10+2 (Intermediate) pass from any recognized board.
Peon / Orderly / Chowkidar / Safai Karamchari 10+2 pass. Merit is built from 10+2 marks (converted out of 85) plus a document-evaluation score (out of 15).

There's a local-knowledge clause here that a lot of applicants tend to overlook — candidates need familiarity with the customs and dialects of Himachal Pradesh, and Group-C posts require matric/10+2/graduation, while Group-D posts require middle/matric/10+2 schooling from an institution located within HP. Bonafide Himachali candidates are exempt from the institution-location part of this rule, but the domicile requirement itself still applies to everyone.

Selection Process

The overall selection rests on a Merit List, Document Verification, and (for some posts) a Medical Examination — but each post has its own specific test in between:

  • Court Manager: Written Test + Viva-voce
  • Clerk: Screening Test → Written Test → Typing Test → Document Verification
  • Stenographer Grade-III: Screening Test → Stenography Test (80 WPM) → Typing Test
  • Driver: Screening Test → Driving Proficiency Test → Document Verification
  • Process Server: Screening Test → Written Test → Evaluation
  • Peon and other Group-D posts: Straight merit list built from educational marks plus document evaluation, no written test involved

  • Recent coloured photograph (20–50 KB, JPG/PNG, white background)
  • Signature (10–20 KB, JPG/PNG, white background)
  • Matriculation certificate as age proof (100–500 KB)
  • ID Proof — Aadhaar, Driving Licence, or Passport (100–500 KB)
  • Remaining educational/experience/category certificates in PDF format (100 KB to 2 MB)

How to Apply

  1. Register on the recruitment portal at hphcrecruitment.in/login.
  2. Fill in your category, post, and district preference carefully — apply only once per post; there's no need for separate Regular/Contract/Daily Wages applications.
  3. Scan and upload the required documents, staying within the size limits.
  4. Pay the applicable fee through online mode.
  5. Preview the form before final submission — once submitted, it can't be withdrawn or edited, only cancelled (without a refund).
  6. Keep a printout or screenshot of your final submission for your own records.

Important Links

Apply Online hphcrecruitment.in/login
Official Notification PDF highcourt.hp.gov.in (Recruitment section)
Official Website highcourt.hp.gov.in

Preparation Strategy — Post-Wise, Not "Just Study Hard"

Clerk and Process Server are going to see the heaviest competition of the lot, because Clerk is an open graduate-level post and Process Server needs only 10+2 — which means the applicant pool for both is enormous. For Clerk aspirants, the single most critical factor is typing: 30 WPM in English and 25 WPM in Hindi on the Kruti Dev font, which has a completely different key layout compared to Mangal or other Unicode fonts. If you've never practiced on Kruti Dev before, start now with an online typing tutor and build actual muscle memory rather than trying to memorize key positions — this isn't a two-week job, it usually takes a good month.

The Stenographer post is the toughest one on this entire list — 80 WPM shorthand speed is on par with UPSC or State PSC-level stenographer exams. For candidates already preparing for another steno exam, this is a natural add-on; for someone starting from scratch, hitting that speed in less than five or six months isn't really realistic, honestly.

For Driver, the licence and experience are the real filter, not the exam itself — if you don't already have 3 years of LMV driving experience, double-check whether it'll actually be complete by the last date before you apply.

Peon and the other Group-D posts skip the written test entirely — merit comes straight from 10+2 marks plus a handful of extra evaluation points (BPL status, backward-area residence, NCC certificate, and so on). Which means for these posts, "preparation" mostly means getting your eligible certificates in order well in advance, not opening a textbook.

Should You Apply?

If you're an HP domicile candidate, a graduate, and your typing or steno skills are already above average — both Clerk and Stenographer are worth applying for, and given the low fee, the downside is minimal. If you're only 10+2 pass and don't have a driving licence or driving experience, Process Server or Peon posts are the better fit since there's no high-skill barrier there.

For candidates deep into preparation for a State PSC or SSC exam already, it might make more sense to treat this as a "side apply" — the Clerk and Steno selection process demands a completely different skillset (typing/stenography), and general knowledge or reasoning prep won't transfer over directly here. If you already have Kruti Dev typing speed, it's absolutely worth a shot; if not, whether it's worth investing the time now is something you'll have to weigh against your own exam calendar.

How many total vacancies are there in the HP High Court Various Post Recruitment 2026?

There are 388 posts in total, with Clerk (141) and Peon/Orderly (89) accounting for the largest share — together they make up well over half the total vacancies.

What is the last date for application and fee payment?

Both close on 10 September 2026 at 11:59 PM — the fee-payment window shuts along with the application, there's no separate extra time for it.

Is this recruitment for the High Court's own staff or for district courts?

This is specifically for District Judiciary Staff (R&P Rules, 2022), posted across civil and sessions divisions all over Himachal — the High Court's own establishment recruitment (R&P Rules, 2015) is a separate service, and its post count is usually much smaller (a January 2025 drive under that service had only 14 posts).

What's the difference between Regular and Contract mode for Clerk and Stenographer posts?

Regular posts come with a defined pay level (Level-03 for Clerk, for instance), while Contract-mode wages are fixed by the Govt. of HP from time to time — both are filled through the same selection process, only the appointment mode differs.

When will the exam date be announced?

The notification currently just says "Notify Soon," with no tentative date given — candidates should keep checking the official website regularly, since all communication is sent only via SMS and email.

Is the age limit for the Court Manager post the same as the other posts?

No, this is the biggest exception — every other post falls in the 18–45/50 range, but Court Manager is restricted to candidates aged 25 to 35, with no relaxation mentioned either way.

Can candidates without HP domicile apply?

Technically, any Indian citizen can apply, but the lower reserved-category fee is only for HP domicile candidates, and Group-C/D posts also carry a local-schooling clause from which only bonafide Himachali candidates are exempt.

This post has been put together purely for information and analysis. Before applying, please cross-check the official notification and the recruitment portal for the latest updates — dates, vacancy numbers, or eligibility conditions can be revised by the High Court at any time.

Prep Strategy — What Matters Right Now

Form's in, correction window's closed — none of that logistics stuff matters anymore. What matters is Prelims, five weeks out, and Prelims is just three sections: English, Numerical Ability, Reasoning. 35 marks each for the last two, 30 for English, 60 minutes on the clock. Everyone throws hours at Reasoning because it feels like something you can visibly get better at. Fair. But English comprehension is usually where the real damage happens quietly — people assume they're fine at English because reading a sentence like this one poses no problem, then completely freeze on an actual comprehension passage once the timer starts running.

Mains is the real filter, though, and this is where people mess up the timeline. General and Financial Awareness gets shelved until two weeks before the exam, and by then it's genuinely too late — you can't absorb six months of banking news in fourteen days, you can only memorise headlines you'll forget the week after. Twenty minutes a day, starting today, does more than any cram session ever will. Computer Knowledge is the same story — pure memory, not logic, so steady daily revision beats one exhausting weekend before the exam.

One thing people underestimate: whatever state you picked while filling the form is the language you get tested on in the Local Language Proficiency Test, after Mains. If you can speak that state's language but can't really read or write it well, deal with that now, over the next month — not after your Mains result lands and you suddenly realise there's a problem.

Should You Take This Attempt Seriously?

Since the forms are closed, this question is really about how much weight this attempt should carry against your other bank exams this season. If your English is already solid and your quant/reasoning speed is decent, treat this one as the real deal — 11,403 seats is a lot more room than a lean year gives you, and cutoffs should reflect that.

If your speed's still a work in progress, don't dismiss this attempt as just a mock either. The syllabus barely changes across IBPS Clerk, SBI Clerk, and RRB Office Assistant, so anything you sharpen here carries straight into the next exam. And honestly — if English comprehension is your weak spot, fix that one first. It quietly costs you marks in every bank exam this season, not just this one.

So how many vacancies are we actually talking about for CSA-XVI 2026?

11,403 posts, spread across 11 public sector banks. Canara Bank alone takes 2,500 of them — the biggest chunk by far.

Can I still apply, or has the window closed?

It's closed — 28 August 2026 was the final date, after IBPS pushed it back a week from 21 August. The correction window on 4–5 September is over too, so there's genuinely nothing left to edit for this cycle.

Does the Prelims score actually count toward anything?

Not really — it's just a qualifying hurdle. Your Mains score is what decides your rank and, eventually, which bank you get allotted to.

Do I need to sit through an interview at some point?

No, and this catches a lot of people off guard, especially if they've come from SSC-type exams. After Mains, it's just the Local Language Test and document verification — nobody's sitting across a table asking you questions.

Why do SC/ST/PwBD candidates pay a different fee?

General, OBC, and EWS candidates pay ₹850; SC, ST, PwBD, and Ex-servicemen pay a much smaller ₹175. For what it's worth, SBI's Clerk drive this year takes it a step further and drops the fee entirely for SC/ST/PwBD/ESM applicants.

Is this actually more seats than last year, or does it just sound bigger?

It's genuinely more. Last year's cycle (CSA-XV) had around 10,277 vacancies based on available records, so this year's 11,403 works out to roughly an 11% jump.

What kind of salary should I actually expect in hand?

Basic pay is ₹24,050 to start, but once DA, HRA, and other allowances get added in, most people end up seeing somewhere between ₹40,000 and ₹46,000 a month, depending on where they're posted.

A quick heads-up before you go: none of this is set in stone. IBPS has a habit of tweaking dates, fees, and vacancy numbers with little warning, so before you act on anything here, it's worth cross-checking against the official notification on ibps.in.

Preparing for TRE 4.0: What Actually Matters

Your first checkpoint isn't the exam — it's your eligibility test. CTET/BTET Paper I for Classes 1-5, STET Paper I for Classes 6-10, and STET Paper II for Classes 11-12. If you haven't cleared the relevant paper yet, that's the actual bottleneck, not the BPSC written exam itself. Bihar has run STET cycles fairly regularly, so check if a valid scorecard is sitting with you already before you assume you need to start from zero.

Once eligibility's sorted, the Mains exam is where the real competition happens. Previous TRE cycles have generally treated the preliminary round as a qualifying screen rather than something that adds to your final merit score, with Mains marks alone deciding the cutoff. That pattern seems likely to hold here too, though it's worth double-checking against the syllabus PDF once BPSC drops it, since these things do occasionally get revised.

Given how PGT (Classes 11-12) has swelled to 16,101 seats this cycle, candidates with a postgraduate degree and STET Paper II clearance should treat this as their strongest window in years. If you already hold a Bihar STET certificate from an earlier cycle and it's still within its validity window, you've got a real head start over candidates who need to clear it fresh. Check your certificate's validity date first; STET scorecards don't stay valid indefinitely.

Honestly, if you're a primary-level (Classes 1-5) aspirant sitting on the fence because the vacancy count looks smaller than TRE 3.0's, apply anyway. 3,847 is still a real number of openings, and BPSC's history suggests final vacancy counts sometimes get revised upward closer to the exam.

CTET or BTET Paper I for Classes 1-5, STET Paper I for Classes 6-10, and STET Paper II specifically for Classes 11-12 — these aren't interchangeable, so double-check which one your target post requires.

The 2024 cycle (CEN 02/2024) opened with 9,144 vacancies and then, through a corrigendum later that year, grew all the way to 14,298 once RRB added 22 fresh trade categories. Whether this cycle sees a similar mid-process expansion is anyone's guess — RRB doesn't announce that in advance — but candidates comparing this year's prospects to 2024's shouldn't assume the same scale of opportunity without that later boost actually happening again.

What makes Technician recruitment genuinely different from most Railway exams is the split personality of the post itself. Technician Grade I Signal and Technician Grade III are announced under the same CEN number, share the same application portal, and go through the same three broad stages — but they're really two separate recruitments wearing one notification. Grade I wants a diploma or engineering degree; Grade III wants a Class 10 pass plus an ITI certificate. The exam papers aren't even the same. Treating this as "one exam" because it's one notification is where a lot of candidates go wrong before they've even started preparing.

This piece breaks down every field from the notification, checks the vacancy trend against the last couple of cycles, and gets into what's actually different about prepping for Grade III versus Grade I Signal.
