What the Vacancy Drop From 2024 Actually Tells You

2024's Technician cycle is worth studying closely because it didn't stay at its opening number. RRB started with 9,144 vacancies (1,092 for Grade I, 8,052 for Grade III), then issued a corrigendum months later adding 22 new trade categories and pushing Grade III alone up to 13,206 — a final combined total of 14,298. This year's opening figure of 6,557 is well below even that initial 2024 number, let alone the expanded one. There's no way to know in advance whether RRB will repeat that pattern this cycle, but the precedent exists, so don't treat 6,557 as a hard ceiling the way you might for a first-time notification with no recent history of mid-cycle expansion.

Prep Strategy — Grade I and Grade III Need Genuinely Different Prep

If you're targeting Grade III, General Science carries the heaviest weight at 40 of 100 marks, and this section tends to lean on basic Physics, Chemistry, and Biology at a Class 10 level rather than anything specialised to your trade — the trade knowledge itself isn't directly tested in the CBT. Mathematics and Reasoning together make up half the remaining marks, so standard RRB-level arithmetic and pattern-based reasoning practice covers most of your prep needs here. Grade I Signal flips that weighting almost entirely — Basic Science & Engineering alone is 35 marks, and Computers adds another 20, meaning 55 of 100 marks come from technical and computing knowledge rather than general aptitude. If you're coming from a diploma background, lean into your core subjects hard; if you're coming from a straight B.Sc., make sure your applied engineering concepts (not just theoretical physics) are solid, since that's closer to what this paper actually tests.

Should You Apply?

If your ITI trade matches one of the higher-vacancy categories here — Carriage & Wagon, Diesel Mechanical, or Fitter, going by the numbers — this is genuinely one of the more accessible Railway technical entries running right now, especially since it's a single-CBT process rather than the multi-stage grind ALP puts you through. Honestly, if your trade certificate is in a niche category with a handful of seats, don't rule it out either — smaller vacancy counts in specific trades often mean a much smaller applicant pool too, since not everyone qualifies for every category.

If you're eligible for Grade I Signal on paper but your actual comfort with engineering-level Physics and applied electronics is shaky, think twice before banking everything on this one exam — 323 seats nationally is a tight field, and the paper doesn't give you much room to lean on general aptitude the way Grade III's paper does. Building genuine subject depth over the next few months matters more here than just grinding practice sets.

Is Technician Grade I Signal and Grade III the same exam, since they're under one notification?

No — they run under the same CEN number and portal, but the eligibility, exam pattern, and pay level are completely different, so check which grade you actually qualify for before assuming both are open to you.

How does this year's vacancy count compare to the last Technician cycle?

This cycle opened with 6,557 posts, well below 2024's initial 9,144 — and 2024 later grew to 14,298 through a corrigendum, so this year's final number could still shift depending on whether RRB follows that same pattern.

Do I get my application fee back if I don't clear the exam?

You get part of it back regardless of your result — ₹400 for General/OBC and the full ₹250 for SC/ST/PwBD/Women/Ex-servicemen — but only if you actually appear for the CBT; missing the exam after paying means no refund at all.

Can I apply for both Grade I Signal and Grade III in the same cycle?

The notification treats them as separate eligibility tracks based on your qualification, so whether you can apply to both depends on whether you genuinely meet both sets of educational criteria — check the detailed notification's post-parameters annexure rather than assuming automatic eligibility for both.

Is there a correction window if I make a mistake in my form?

Yes, from 1 to 10 August 2026, but it comes with a separate ₹250 correction charge on top of whatever fee you already paid.

Which trade has the most seats this cycle?

Based on available records, Fitter (PU & Workshop) leads with over 1,100 posts, followed by Carriage & Wagon at 501 — though the exhaustive trade list runs to around 39 categories, so check the full annexure for your specific trade.

What's the minimum qualifying percentage I need in the CBT?

It depends on your category — 40% for UR and EWS, 30% for OBC-NCL and SC, and 25% for ST — and this threshold applies the same way to both Grade I and Grade III papers.

Everything above reflects CEN 02/2026 as published and reported at the time of writing. Trade-wise and zone-wise vacancy splits, exam dates, and even total vacancy counts have shifted through corrigenda in past Technician cycles, so it's worth checking the detailed notification on your regional RRB website before finalising your trade preference or travel plans for the exam.

Why JNU's Approach Looks Different

Compare this to how Delhi University handles non-teaching hiring. Each college runs its own separate notification, whenever it needs to. Dyal Singh College just put out 33 posts, some other college did 11, another did 4 — small batches, spread through the year, no fixed rhythm to it. BHU works similarly. JNU, this time, bundled everything into one centralized notification covering every school and department at once. That's the real difference. Reasoning and Maths carry the heaviest weight, 70 marks each, and it would be a mistake to go easy on them just because this is technically a "non-teaching staff" exam. Out of 150 questions, 35 each belong to these two sections alone, so both need serious attention. With negative marking in play, guessing needs to be calculated rather than random — wrong answers cost you.

Paper II's domain-specific portion changes depending on the post — a Stenographer might see questions on office procedure or typing conventions, a Statistical Assistant gets basic statistics, a Computer Operator faces programming or networking fundamentals. Look up the syllabus specific to your post in the notification PDF; generic prep won't cut it for this paper.

For anyone facing a skill test — Stenographer, PA, Private Secretary, Assistant, Junior Assistant — here's one thing worth knowing: there often isn't much of a gap between clearing the written test and the skill test being scheduled. Start building your typing or shorthand speed now rather than waiting until after the written result comes out.

Junior Executive (Survey & Cartography) B.E./B.Tech in Civil Engineering, or M.Sc. in Geography, Remote Sensing & GIS, Geo-informatics, or Geomatics — no experience required

How to Actually Prepare for This One

The CBT here isn't discipline-agnostic like a banking prelims exam. From what's known of the pattern, Part A carries around 30% weightage and covers general knowledge, reasoning, and aptitude — the usual stuff you'd expect. Part B, though, is where the real weightage sits, and it's entirely built around your specific discipline. That changes your prep priorities completely. Spending three months polishing your English or reasoning section, while ignoring core subject revision, would be a mistake here — unlike SSC or banking exams where general sections often decide the cutoff.

There's no negative marking in this CBT, which honestly should change how you attempt the paper. Don't leave questions blank out of fear the way you might in an RRB or SSC exam. Attempt everything you can make an educated guess on; there's genuinely nothing to lose.

If you're applying for Manager posts, start building your interview narrative now, not after the CBT result. AAI's interview panel for management-cadre posts typically probes actual project or work experience in depth — vague answers about "handling a team" won't cut it. Get specific: numbers, outcomes, what you personally owned versus what your team did collectively.

And if you're eyeing Operations or Fire Services, don't wait till the last month to check your Light Motor Vehicle licence status. Fire Services candidates additionally need to start basic physical conditioning early — running, rope climbing, pole climbing are all part of the Physical Efficiency stages, and these aren't things you can cram for in a week.

Should You Apply? Here's How to Think About It

If you're a fresh graduate with no work experience, your realistic options are limited to the four Junior Executive streams: Finance, Law, Operations, or Survey & Cartography. Don't waste your ₹1,000 fee applying to a Manager post you're not eligible for — check the experience clause twice before submitting.

If you've got 3+ years of relevant experience and hold a niche qualification like Architecture or Corporate Planning, apply, but go in with your eyes open about how thin those seats are. One or two vacancies nationwide means a single strong competitor from a metro city with better exposure could edge you out, regardless of how good your CBT score is.

If you're mid-prep for SBI PO or another banking exam and happen to hold an MBA Finance, CA, or CMA qualification, there's a decent case for applying here too. The single-CBT format doesn't demand a separate multi-month prep track, and the pay scale for Manager (Finance) roles is genuinely competitive with junior banking positions.

Honestly, if you're targeting the Corporate Communications or Corporate Planning seats specifically because they "sound easy," reconsider. Fewer vacancies almost always mean the applicant pool per seat is more concentrated with genuinely qualified niche candidates, not less competitive.

7 September 2026, and that's also the last date for fee payment — there's no separate window for that here, unlike some other PSU drives.

389 in total, with 260 going to Manager-level posts and the remaining 129 to Junior Executive posts across four disciplines.

No, and this trips up a lot of applicants. AAI runs a separate GATE-score-based JE drive for pure engineering disciplines. This 2026 notification is a CBT-based process covering both Manager and JE posts across a much wider mix of fields, including Finance, Law, and Corporate Communications.

Do I need work experience to apply?

Only for Manager posts, where 3 years of relevant post-qualification experience is mandatory. Junior Executive posts have no experience requirement, so freshers can apply there.

No. AAI has confirmed there's no negative marking for wrong answers, so it's worth attempting every question you have even a reasonable guess on.

No, only for Manager posts under Post Codes 1 to 11. Junior Executive candidates go through application verification and other applicable tests instead, but skip the formal interview stage.

Because the role itself demands physical fitness beyond a desk job — candidates go through a Physical Measurement Test, a driving test, and a Physical Endurance Test covering things like rope and pole climbing, on top of the usual CBT and interview.

Before anything else, get one thing straight: this isn't a Railway job. It's training. The North Central Railway notification for 1,853 slots is engagement under the Apprentices Act, 1961 — a one-year skill-training programme, not a permanent post with a pay scale and a pension track. A huge number of 10th-pass and ITI candidates apply here every cycle assuming it's a foot in the door to a Group C Railway career, and in a roundabout way it can be, but the notification itself is blunt about what it isn't promising you.

What makes this cycle worth a proper look is the trend — 1,853 slots this year against 1,763 in the previous NCR apprentice drive from September 2025, a rise of about 90 seats, roughly 5%. Nothing dramatic, but a genuine increase rather than a flat repeat. The minimum age here is also unusually low at 15 years, which tells you this scheme is squarely aimed at candidates straight out of Class 10 and ITI, not adults who've already spent years in the workforce.

This piece runs through every field in the notification, checks the vacancy trend and the fee structure against comparable Act Apprentice drives running in other Railway zones this season, and gets into what actually happens after your one year of training ends — because that part matters more than most candidates realise before they apply.

How This Compares to Other Railway Zone Apprentice Drives

Nearly every Railway zone runs its own Act Apprentice recruitment on its own schedule, so comparing NCR against a couple of parallel zone drives gives a useful sense of scale.

Recruitment Total Slots Fee (Gen-OBC-EWS / Reserved) Age Limit Selection Process

RRC Western Railway Apprentice 2025–26 (RRC/WR/04/2025) 5,349 Fee waived for reserved categories (based on available records) 15–24 years, per standard Apprentices Act norms Merit List (10th + ITI marks) → DV
RRC South Central Railway Apprentice 2026 2,801 Similar structure to other zones (based on available records) 15–24 years Merit List (10th % + ITI % average) → DV

Western Railway's 5,349 slots dwarf NCR's count, but that's mostly a function of WR simply covering more workshops and divisions, not any difference in how competitive the scheme is per seat. What's consistent across every zone, NCR included, is the complete absence of a written exam — this entire selection runs on your existing Class 10 and ITI marksheets, so your prep for this "exam" already happened years ago, whether you realised it at the time or not.

  • Duration: 1 year of practical training under the Apprentices Act.
  • Stipend: not specified in this short notice, but based on how comparable RRC zone apprenticeships have structured stipends for the current training year, apprentices typically receive somewhere around ₹7,000 to ₹9,600 per month, varying by trade — treat this as an approximate range rather than a confirmed NCR figure until the detailed notification or your offer letter confirms it.
  • No HRA, DA, or travel allowance applies — this is a fixed training stipend, not a regular salary structure.

  3. Fill in your personal, educational, and trade-certificate details in the online form.

What Happens After Your Training Year Ends

This is the part most candidates skip over, and it's genuinely the most important context for deciding whether to apply. The notification format for Act Apprentice schemes across every Railway zone carries a standard line: training under this scheme confers no automatic right to absorption into Railway service, and it isn't obligatory for the Railway to offer employment once your year is up. That's not unique to NCR — it's how the Apprentices Act works everywhere.

That said, it's not a dead end either. Railway Board's own circular (RBE No. 71/2016) earmarks 20% of direct-recruitment vacancies in Level 1 posts — the erstwhile Pay Band-1, Grade Pay ₹1,800 category, which covers roles like Track Maintainer and similar entry-level technical posts — for preference to Course Completed Act Apprentices holding a National Apprenticeship Certificate from NCVT. In practice, this means your year here can genuinely improve your odds in a future RRB Group D or Level 1 recruitment cycle, even though it guarantees nothing on its own. Treat the certificate as a real, if modest, edge — not a golden ticket, and not worthless either.

Prep Strategy — There's No Exam, So Prep Means Something Different Here

Since your Class 10 and ITI percentages are what actually decide your merit rank, there's genuinely nothing left to "study" for this recruitment — whatever marks you scored years ago are locked in. What you can control right now is accuracy in the application itself: entering your marksheet percentages correctly, uploading the right certificate scans, and picking your preferred division or trade carefully if the form allows a preference order. A transposed digit in your ITI percentage, or a mismatched certificate upload, is a far more realistic risk to your selection chances here than anything exam-related. If your ITI percentage is on the lower side, it's worth applying anyway rather than skipping the cycle — merit cutoffs vary by trade and division, and a trade with fewer applicants relative to seats can pull a candidate through with a percentage that wouldn't clear a more popular trade.

Should You Apply?

If you're a Class 10 pass with an ITI certificate in a relevant trade and you're genuinely early in your career — the 15-year minimum age tells you this scheme wants candidates fresh out of their ITI course — this is a low-cost, low-risk way to get real workshop experience and a National Apprenticeship Certificate that carries some weight in future Railway recruitment. The ₹100 fee, or zero fee if you fall in an exempt category, makes this an easy application to file even as a backup alongside other exams you're prepping for.

Honestly, if you're already holding down full-time work or expecting this apprenticeship to function as a guaranteed job with a proper salary, this isn't the right fit — the stipend is modest, there's no allowance structure, and nothing here is contractually promised beyond the training itself. Treat it as a stepping stone toward a future RRB or RRC recruitment, not as the destination.

Is this Act Apprentice programme an actual Railway job with a salary?

No — it's a one-year training engagement under the Apprentices Act with a fixed monthly stipend, not a regular post with a pay scale, and the notification explicitly doesn't promise employment once training ends.

Is there a written exam I need to prepare for?

No, selection runs entirely on a merit list built from your existing Class 10 and ITI marks — there's no CBT, no interview, and nothing new to study for this particular recruitment.

How does this cycle's vacancy count compare to last time?

1,853 slots this year against 1,763 in the previous NCR apprentice cycle from late 2025 — a modest but real increase of roughly 5%, not a dramatic jump.

Does completing this apprenticeship help me get a permanent Railway job later?

It can — Railway Board policy sets aside 20% of Level 1 direct-recruitment vacancies as preference seats for Course Completed Act Apprentices with a National Apprenticeship Certificate, though it doesn't guarantee automatic absorption on its own.

Do all candidates pay the same application fee?

No — General, OBC, and EWS candidates pay ₹100, while SC, ST, PH, and all female candidates across every category apply completely free of charge.

Why is the minimum age as low as 15 years for this recruitment?

Because this scheme specifically targets candidates who've just finished Class 10 and an ITI course, which many complete well before turning 18 — this isn't a typo, it genuinely differs from most Railway recruitment where the floor is 18.

What if my trade isn't listed among the higher-vacancy categories?

Smaller vacancy counts in a specific trade often come with a proportionally smaller applicant pool too, so don't assume a low seat number automatically means a tougher cutoff — check the detailed notification's trade-wise annexure for your specific division before deciding.

The figures and dates above reflect the RRC/NCR/01/2026 notification and comparable zone-wise data as available at the time of writing. Division-wise and trade-wise vacancy splits, along with merit list and document verification dates, are usually released in follow-up notices on rrcpryj.org, so it's worth checking the official site directly rather than relying on this or any other single summary before you finalise your application.

CBT-1 and CBT-2 test genuinely different things, so lumping your prep into one generic "study everything" bucket wastes time you don't have.

General Awareness here leans toward static GK and recent current affairs; General Science stays at a basic, non-technical level, so don't over-invest depth here at the cost of your technical prep for CBT-2.

CBT-2 is where your actual engineering knowledge gets tested, and it's discipline-specific — meaning a Civil candidate's technical portion looks nothing like an Electrical candidate's. Pull the syllabus for your specific post rather than generic "RRB JE syllabus" content floating around, since Technical Abilities marks carry real weight toward final merit here, unlike CBT-1.

Environment & Pollution and Basics of Computer Applications in CBT-2 often get treated as afterthoughts, and that's a mistake — they're fixed-content sections that reward straightforward revision far more efficiently than the technical portion does per hour invested. Physical Tests (Where Applicable)

Why do different sources show different application dates for JILCCE-2026?

Ten seats. That's the entire vacancy count for this JAG 125th Entry cycle, and if you're a law graduate scrolling past this thinking it's too small a number to bother with, you might want to pause. Compare it to the 124th course that closed earlier this year — that one had just 8 combined vacancies. This cycle bumps it back up to 10, split evenly at 5 for men and 5 for women, matching the 123rd course from earlier in 2026. So while the number looks tiny next to something like an SSC CGL or a state PSC drive, in the world of JAG entries, 10 is actually on the higher end of what's been on offer lately.

What really sets this entry apart, though, isn't the vacancy count — it's the selection method. There's no written exam here. None. Shortlisting for the SSB interview happens purely on your CLAT PG 2026 score, the one you sat for back in December 2025. That's a genuinely unusual route into a commissioned defence post, and it means your law school performance and CLAT PG rank matter more than anything you'd cram for in the next few weeks. If your CLAT PG score wasn't great, this particular door might already be narrower than it looks on paper, no matter how well you'd otherwise do in an SSB.

Competition-wise, expect it to be sharp among candidates who did clear a strong CLAT PG rank — because everyone in that bracket across the country is eligible to apply for these same 10 seats. Unlike a state-level exam where geography narrows the pool, this is genuinely pan-India, unmarried men and women both, and law schools across the country will have graduates eyeing this. Honestly, if your CLAT PG rank was mediocre and you're hoping the SSB will somehow carry you through, that's a risky bet — shortlisting ratios for JAG have historically been tight given how few seats exist.

Indian Army JAG vs Other Defence Officer Entries for Graduates

Look at that fee row and vacancy row together, and the picture gets interesting. JAG has zero fee and the smallest seat count by a huge margin, while AFCAT charges ₹550 and has thirty-plus times the seats. If pure numbers-game odds matter to you, AFCAT or Navy SSC branches open up more room. But if you specifically want to practice law within the armed forces rather than administration, logistics, or a technical stream, JAG remains the only direct legal-officer entry — there just isn't a substitute route for it.

Selection Process, Training & Pay — What the Notification Doesn't Spell Out in One Place

Since the source notification is light on selection-stage and salary detail beyond eligibility and dates, it's worth laying this out clearly based on how the JAG entry scheme has consistently run in recent cycles: shortlisting for the SSB happens purely on your CLAT PG 2026 score, followed by a five-day SSB interview, then a medical examination, and finally a merit list. There's no separate written test at any stage — that's the defining feature of this entry route compared to almost every other defence commission. Selected candidates undergo 49 weeks of pre-commission training at the Officers Training Academy (OTA), Chennai, after which they're awarded a Short Service Commission as Lieutenant in Pay Level 10 (₹56,100–₹1,77,500) along with Military Service Pay and other allowances. Training also earns you a PG Diploma in Defence Management and Strategic Studies from the University of Madras, which isn't nothing if you're thinking about a second career path down the line.

Candidates should always cross-check dates, eligibility criteria, and CLAT PG exam requirements against the official Indian Army notification before applying — schedules and category-wise relaxation details can shift, and this summary reflects information available at the time of writing.

Preparation Strategy — What Actually Matters Here

Since there's no written paper standing between you and the SSB, your prep energy needs to go almost entirely toward the interview and psychological testing stages, not toward revising bare acts.

Sharpen your grip on legal reasoning and constitutional law fundamentals anyway — not because there's an exam on it, but because SSB panels for JAG entries do probe subject knowledge conversationally, and a hollow "I have an LLB but can't explain basic constitutional provisions" moment doesn't land well. Revise core LLB subjects like Constitutional Law, Criminal Law, and Contract Law at a level where you can discuss them naturally, not recite them.

Stay current on recent Supreme Court and High Court judgments too. Panels sometimes ask about recent legal developments just to see how you think on your feet, and candidates who follow legal news regularly tend to handle those questions with more ease than those cramming case names the night before.

Physical fitness genuinely can't be an afterthought. The SSB includes physical and psychological tests spread across its five days, and candidates who show up unprepared physically tend to struggle more than they expect, regardless of how strong their legal background is. Start a basic fitness routine well before your SSB dates get confirmed rather than scrambling in the final week.

Group discussions and mock interviews deserve real practice time as well — not a one-off session, but repeated rounds. The Personality Assessment stage rewards candidates who can articulate their thoughts clearly under mild pressure, and that skill builds with repetition more than with any single day of prep.

Should You Apply? A Decision Framework

Apply if: you're an unmarried law graduate with a solid LLB percentage above the 55% threshold, you appeared for CLAT PG 2026 and got a competitive score, and you're genuinely drawn to a legal career inside the armed forces rather than corporate law or litigation. If you meet all three of those, there's very little reason to skip this — the fee is zero, so the only real cost is your time and effort in the SSB prep.

If you're still unmarried but weren't able to sit for CLAT PG 2026 at all, unfortunately this cycle isn't for you — that requirement isn't flexible, and there's no backdoor around it. Wait for a future cycle and make sure you register for the next CLAT PG well in advance.

Honestly, if your CLAT PG rank was on the lower side, apply anyway since there's no fee and nothing to lose — but temper your expectations, because with only 10 seats nationwide, shortlisting ratios will likely stay tight. Candidates who cleared CLAT PG comfortably and also have decent physical fitness and communication skills going into the SSB are the ones with realistically strong odds this cycle.

Is there any written exam for the JAG 125th Entry?

No — this is one of the few defence officer entries that skips a written exam entirely. Shortlisting for the SSB is based purely on your CLAT PG 2026 score.

How many vacancies are available this time compared to the last cycle?

This cycle has 10 combined vacancies (5 men, 5 women), up from the 124th course's 8 combined vacancies earlier in 2026 — so the seat count has actually improved slightly.

Is there any application fee for this recruitment?

None at all — General, OBC, EWS, SC, ST, and female candidates all apply completely free of cost for this entry.

Can married law graduates apply for JAG 125th Entry?

No, this entry is open only to unmarried male and unmarried female candidates, and this condition typically needs to hold through the training period as well.

What happens if I didn't appear for CLAT PG 2026?

You won't be eligible for this specific cycle, since a valid CLAT PG 2026 score is a mandatory requirement, not an optional advantage — there's no alternate qualifying route.

What training do selected candidates go through, and what do they earn while training?

Selected candidates undergo 49 weeks of pre-commission training at OTA Chennai and also earn a PG Diploma in Defence Management and Strategic Studies from the University of Madras on completion.

What's the last time to submit the application on the final day?

Applications close strictly at 3:00 PM on 17 August 2026, not at midnight like many other government recruitment portals — a detail candidates sometimes miss and regret.

If you play an instrument and can also stomach a Physical Fitness Test, this is about as niche as government recruitment gets. The Indian Air Force Band isn't hiring thousands of people — it's hiring musicians, and the entire selection hinges on things no other Agnipath stream asks for: tempo, pitch, singing a full song from memory, reading a music notation system. A candidate who's a brilliant Class 10 student but can't hold a tune doesn't get anywhere close to this one, regardless of marks.

Before anything else, here's a mix-up worth clearing right away. The Air Force has released two entirely separate things this cycle that both carry the label "Intake 01/2027" — the main Agniveer Vayu recruitment (open to Science, Maths, and vocational-stream candidates, roughly 3,000 seats, registration back in January–March 2026) and this Musician-specific rally, which opened in July 2026 with its own dates, its own eligibility, and its own selection process entirely. They are not the same recruitment. If you already applied to the general Agniveer Vayu drive earlier this year, that has no bearing on this one — you'd need to register separately for the Musician rally.

Admit cards for this Musician intake went out on 17 August 2026, and the actual rally — where the testing happens — runs from 31 August to 9 September 2026 at two locations only: Air Force Station New Delhi and 7 ASC in Bengaluru. No exam centre choice here, unlike most other government exams; you go to whichever of the two the Air Force assigns you, or the one you selected during registration.

How This Stacks Up Against Other Agnipath Streams

All three services run Agnipath recruitment, but the entry paths look nothing alike once you get into specifics — vacancy scale, fee, even how age is calculated differs meaningfully.

Recruitment Approx. Vacancies Application Fee Age Window Selection Stages
IAF Agniveer Vayu (Musician) Intake 01/2027 Not specified in the notification ₹100 + 18% GST Unmarried, born 1 Jan 2005 – 1 July 2009 (17.5–21 yrs at enrolment) Music Proficiency Test → English Written Test → PFT → Adaptability Test-II → Medical
IAF Agniveer Vayu (general) Intake 01/2027 ~3,000 (based on available reports) ₹550–₹649 + GST 17.5–21 years, born 1 Jan 2006 – 1 July 2009 Online Exam → PFT → Medical → Adaptability Test
Indian Army Agniveer CCE 2026 25,000+ ₹250 17.5–21/24 years, post-dependent Written Exam (CEE) → Physical Test → Medical Test

The scale difference alone tells you something — Army's Agniveer intake is a genuinely mass recruitment, Air Force's general Vayu intake is comfortably mid-sized, and this Musician rally sits in a category of its own where the Air Force hasn't even bothered publishing a headline vacancy figure, because the Band's requirement each year comes down to a handful of specific instrument vacancies rather than a round number worth advertising.

The Notification, Field by Field

Important Dates

Online Application Last Date 2 August 2026, 11:00 PM

Application Fee

  • All candidates, regardless of category: ₹100/-
  • Plus 18% GST on top, non-refundable — so the actual amount paid works out closer to ₹118.

This is notably cheaper than the general Agniveer Vayu fee (₹550–₹649 depending on the cycle), likely because the Musician stream draws far fewer applicants and doesn't need the same processing infrastructure.

Age Limit

  • Candidates must be unmarried and born between 1 January 2005 and 1 July 2009 (both dates inclusive).
  • General rule for this stream: minimum 17.5 years, maximum 21 years, as on date of enrolment — not as on the application deadline.
  • Age relaxation applies "as per Indian Air Force regulations," though the notification doesn't spell out category-wise figures.

Total Vacancy

Not specified. The notification and the short-form notice both leave this as "N/A" — unlike the general Agniveer Vayu intake, where an approximate figure (around 3,000) circulates through media coverage, the Musician stream's seat count isn't published as a headline number in the notification itself. It's worth treating this recruitment as a specialised, low-volume rally rather than assuming any round figure applies.

Eligibility

Criterion Requirement
Educational Qualification Passed Matriculation/10th or equivalent, minimum pass marks, from a Government-recognised school or board.
Music Ability Correct tempo and pitch; must be able to sing a full song, perform a preparatory tune, and use at least one music notation system; must play at least one instrument.
Musical Experience Grade 5 or higher from a recognised music institute, OR a diploma in Hindustani/Carnatic classical music, OR certificates/awards from recognised music events.
Marital Status Must be unmarried, and undertake not to marry during the four-year Agnipath engagement period.

Mandatory Medical Standards

  • Height — Male: minimum 162 cm. Female: minimum 152 cm (147 cm for candidates from North East or hilly Uttarakhand; 150 cm for Lakshadweep candidates).
  • Chest — Male: minimum 77 cm circumference with 5 cm minimum expansion. Female: minimum 5 cm expansion, well-proportioned and well-developed.
  • Hearing — must be able to hear a forced whisper from 6 metres, each ear tested separately.
  • General health — free from any active, latent, acute, or chronic medical/surgical disability, infection, or skin ailment; fit to serve in any part of the world, in any climate or terrain.

Selection Process

  1. Proficiency Test in Playing Musical Instruments
  2. English Written Test
  3. Physical Fitness Test (PFT)
  4. Adaptability Test-II
  5. Medical Examination

Notice the order here — the music test comes before the written English test, not after. That's the opposite sequence of most defence recruitment, where a written exam usually screens candidates before anything physical or skill-based gets tested. If your instrument skills aren't rally-ready, showing up "to see how far I get" wastes a rally slot and a day's travel, because you're evaluated on music first, not last.

Career Path & What Comes After Selection

  • Selected candidates join the Indian Air Force Band under the Agnipath Scheme for the standard four-year engagement.
  • Up to 25% of the performing batch may be considered for permanent enrolment into the regular airmen cadre, depending on institutional requirements at the end of the term.
  • Pay follows the standard Agniveer structure: Year 1 — ₹30,000 monthly package (₹21,000 in-hand); Year 2 — ₹33,000 (₹23,100 in-hand); Year 3 — ₹36,500 (₹25,550 in-hand); Year 4 — ₹40,000 (₹28,000 in-hand). The remainder goes into a Seva Nidhi corpus, paid out at the end of the four years.

How to Apply

Registration runs entirely online through iafrecruitment.edcil.co.in, with agnipathvayu.cdac.in as the parallel official gateway mentioned in coverage of this cycle. Register with a working email and phone number, fill in personal and educational details, upload the required documents, photograph, and signature, and pay the fee online before the deadline. No offline submission is accepted under any circumstance — this is standard across all Agnipath streams, not unique to Musician intake.

How This Cycle Compares to Recent Musician Rallies

The Air Force runs this Musician rally roughly once a year, and looking at the last two cycles gives a decent sense of the pattern: Intake 01/2025 held its rally from 3–12 July 2024 at Kanpur and Bengaluru, with candidates born between 2 January 2004 and 2 July 2007 eligible. Intake 01/2026 moved the rally to 10–18 June 2025, shifted the venue from Kanpur to Delhi, and covered candidates born between 1 January 2005 and 1 July 2008. This year's Intake 01/2027 keeps Delhi and Bengaluru as the two venues, pushes the rally slightly later into the year (31 August–9 September), and the eligible birth window (1 January 2005–1 July 2009) runs a full year longer at the upper end than the previous cycle did. Vacancy counts for this specific stream haven't been published in any of the three cycles, so there's no seat-count trend to point to — only the venue and date pattern is genuinely comparable.

Prep Strategy — This One's Different From Every Other Government Exam

Forget generic exam prep advice here; there isn't a syllabus to grind through the way SSC or banking candidates would recognise. Your instrument proficiency is the actual gate, and it's not something you build in the five or six weeks between application and rally — either you already have Grade 5-level training, a classical diploma, or genuine performance history, or you don't. If you're on the fence about whether your skill level qualifies, this is worth an honest conversation with your music teacher before you pay the fee, not after you've travelled to Delhi or Bengaluru.

What you can actually improve in the time you have is the English Written Test and the PFT. The written test isn't detailed section-wise in the notification, but treat it as a basic English comprehension and grammar check rather than anything requiring months of prep. The PFT, on the other hand, rewards weeks of consistent running and basic strength work — 1.6 km run timing and push-ups/sit-ups standards are where candidates with strong musical ability sometimes still get eliminated, simply because they treated fitness as an afterthought next to their instrument practice.

Should You Apply?

If you're a genuinely trained musician — Grade 5 or above, a classical diploma, or real performance credentials — and you meet the 10th-pass and physical standards, this is a legitimate and fairly low-competition route into a stable Air Force career, precisely because the pool of applicants who can actually clear the music test is small to begin with. The ₹100 fee makes it a low-risk shot even as a backup option alongside your other exam prep this season.

If your music background is casual — a few years of guitar lessons as a kid, or singing at family functions — be honest with yourself before applying. The eligibility bar (Grade 5 or a recognised diploma) isn't a formality; it's the actual first filter, and turning up without meeting it isn't going to work out through effort alone on rally day. Put your energy into the general Agniveer Vayu intake or another defence exam instead, where the entry bar is academic rather than a skill you can't cram in six weeks.

Is this the same recruitment as the "Agniveer Vayu Intake 01/2027" that opened back in January 2026?

No — despite sharing the "01/2027" label, that was the general Agniveer Vayu intake for Science/vocational-stream candidates with roughly 3,000 seats, while this Musician rally is a completely separate, smaller recruitment with its own dates and eligibility.

How much does it cost to apply, and is there any category-wise fee difference?

Everyone pays the same ₹100 plus 18% GST — there's no fee waiver for any category here, unlike some other Agnipath streams where SC/ST or women candidates get exemptions.

Do I need to already play in a band or have formal certification to apply?

You need at least one of three things — Grade 5 or higher from a recognised music institute, a diploma in Hindustani or Carnatic classical music, or certificates/awards from recognised music events — informal skill alone won't satisfy the eligibility criteria on paper.

Which comes first at the rally — the music test or the fitness test?

The Proficiency Test in Playing Musical Instruments comes first, ahead of even the English Written Test, so candidates are screened on their actual musical ability before anything else — PFT and Adaptability Test-II follow after.

How many vacancies are actually up for grabs this intake?

The notification doesn't specify a number — unlike the general Agniveer Vayu intake where a rough figure (around 3,000) gets reported, the Musician stream's seat count has never been published as a headline figure across recent cycles either.

What happens after the four-year Agnipath term ends for a Musician Agniveer?

Up to 25% of the performing batch can be considered for permanent enrolment in the regular airmen cadre based on the Air Force's institutional requirements at the time — the rest exit with the Seva Nidhi payout under standard Agnipath terms.

Is there a height relaxation for candidates from smaller or hill states?

Yes — the general minimum height is 162 cm for male candidates, but that drops to 147 cm for candidates from North East states or hilly Uttarakhand, and to 150 cm for candidates from Lakshadweep.

The details above come from the notification and admit card information published for Intake 01/2027 as of this writing. Vacancy figures, exact fee breakdowns, and rally logistics for defence recruitment can shift through addenda even close to the testing dates, so it's worth checking iafrecruitment.edcil.co.in or agnipathvayu.cdac.in directly before you travel for the rally.

Preparation Strategy — Skill-First, Not Syllabus-First

There's no general written paper standing between you and the shorthand test here, so your prep energy needs a completely different shape than a typical 12th-pass government exam.

Speed-build toward the actual thresholds, not past them and not just up to them. English candidates need 80 wpm and Hindi candidates need 70 wpm for a full 6-minute dictation — that's longer than most practice passages people casually drill on. Push your daily practice sessions to at least 8–10 minutes of continuous dictation so the real 6-minute test feels shorter than what you're used to, not equal to it.

Transcription accuracy matters just as much as raw speed. A 5% error margin sounds generous until you realize a single garbled sentence in a 6-minute passage can eat that margin fast. Practice transcribing your own shorthand notes under time pressure — many candidates can take dictation fine but stumble converting it back to clean typed text within the given window.

For the computer test, the Speed and Efficiency components are separately scored with their own qualifying minimums, so don't treat "computer skills" as one blob to revise. Speed Test rewards raw typing pace; Efficiency Test likely checks formatting, accuracy, and possibly basic document handling. Practice both distinctly rather than assuming general typing fluency covers everything.

Honestly, if your shorthand speed currently sits below the required threshold with less than two months to the exam, don't gamble on cramming it up in time — that's not a realistic timeline for building dictation speed from scratch. Consider this cycle as a benchmark test and target the next one seriously instead.

Should You Apply? A Decision Framework

Apply if: your Hindi shorthand is already comfortably above 70 wpm, you hold (or can quickly obtain) an RS-CIT or equivalent computer certificate, and you're a Rajasthan-domiciled candidate eligible for the standard or relaxed age bands. The Grade-III Hindi stream, with 141 of the 163 seats, is genuinely your best shot at these odds.

If your strength leans English rather than Hindi, weigh the numbers honestly — 13 seats is a thin slice, and your competition will be every strong English-shorthand candidate in the state chasing the same small pool. Apply anyway if your speed is solid, but don't count on volume working in your favor the way it might for the Hindi stream.

Wait and build up your skills first if you're not yet hitting the dictation speed thresholds — there's no partial credit for "almost there" in a shorthand test, and reapplying after genuinely getting your speed up beats gambling scarce prep time on this cycle's compressed timeline.

How does this year's vacancy count compare to previous RHC Stenographer cycles?

This cycle has 163 posts, down from 277 in the 2023 recruitment but up slightly from the 144 posts notified in January 2025 — so the trend isn't strictly one-directional.

Do I need a graduation degree to apply?

No — unlike some other High Court stenographer recruitments such as Punjab and Haryana's, which require a B.A. or B.Sc., Rajasthan High Court only asks for a Senior Secondary (12th) pass plus a computer qualification.

What's the fee difference between categories, and is it refundable?

General/OBC/MBC/Other State candidates pay ₹750, OBC-NCL/MBC-NCL/EWS pay ₹600, and SC/ST/PWD pay ₹450 — and like most Rajasthan government exam fees, this isn't refundable once paid, so double-check your category before submitting payment.

Which post has the toughest competition relative to seats?

It's hard to say definitively without applicant data, but with English Grade-III offering only 13 seats against what's likely a smaller but still competitive English-shorthand applicant base, the seat-to-strong-candidate ratio there could be just as tight as the much larger Hindi stream.

What happens during the two-year probation period?

Selected candidates work as Probationer Trainees on a fixed ₹23,700 monthly salary for two years before moving to the regular Pay Matrix Level L-10 scale of ₹33,800–₹1,06,700 — so the starting pay is noticeably lower than the eventual regular scale.

Is the interview stage scored, and does it affect final merit?

No — the interview is qualifying in nature and carries no marks, meaning your final merit ranking comes entirely from the shorthand and computer test scores, not the interview performance.

What age relaxation applies to widows and divorced women specifically?

Widows and divorced women face no upper age limit at all under this notification — a considerably more generous provision than the standard 5-year relaxation given to women candidates generally.

contents.content:
Seven years is a long wait. That's roughly how long it's been since WBPSC last opened up the ICDS Supervisor post back in 2019, and now the commission is finally circling back with a notification that's expected to cover something close to 16,000 posts across Supervisor, Cook, and Helper categories. If you've been tracking West Bengal state exams for a while, you already know this kind of gap between cycles doesn't happen often — and when it does, the backlog of eligible candidates piles up fast.

Here's the thing though: the official notification hasn't dropped yet. What we have right now is a "coming soon" page with expected numbers, tentative age brackets, and a fee structure that's likely carried over from the last cycle. That's not unusual for WBPSC — they tend to put out an advance intimation before the full advertisement, application dates, and post-wise vacancy split get finalized. So treat the specifics below as directionally correct, not gospel, until the PDF notification is actually out.

What makes this round genuinely interesting is the scale. In 2019, WBPSC recruited for just 2,954 Supervisor posts. If the 16,000 figure for this cycle holds even loosely — remember, that number covers Supervisor, Cook, and Helper together, not Supervisor alone — this could turn into one of the bigger women-and-child-development recruitment drives West Bengal has seen in years. Competition for the Supervisor post specifically will still be intense, since it's the only graduate-level, higher-paying role in this bunch and it draws applicants from across the state's B.A./B.Sc./B.Com pool. The Cook and Helper posts, needing just a Class 8 pass, will pull in a completely different applicant base and probably see even sharper competition per seat given the lower eligibility bar.

WBPSC ICDS Supervisor vs Similar Anganwadi Supervisor Recruitments

Qualification Bachelor's degree, any discipline 12th pass (limited recruitment) / Graduate (open recruitment) Class 10th pass

Application Fee ₹160 (General); SC/ST(WB) & PwBD exempted ₹500 (Gen/OBC); ₹250 (SC/ST) No fee for any category
Selection Stages Prelims → Mains (descriptive) → Viva-Voce Written exam → Document verification Merit list based on qualification/experience, largely contract-based
Employment Type Regular govt post Regular/contractual (varies by recruitment mode) Contractual, district-wise

This comparison alone tells you something about where WBPSC's Supervisor post stands. It's the toughest to crack of the three — a three-stage selection with an actual descriptive mains paper is rare for an Anganwadi-linked post. Bihar's version, by contrast, is closer to a contract hiring process with almost no written exam at all, and MP sits somewhere in between. If you're comparing "which state's ICDS supervisor job is easier to get," honestly, West Bengal's isn't it. But it also tends to offer better long-term service conditions once you're in, being a regular post rather than a contractual one.

Preparation Strategy — Stage by Stage

Since the Supervisor post runs on a three-stage selection, your prep plan needs to look different at each stage rather than one generic "revise everything" approach.

Prelims — General Knowledge

Lean hard into West Bengal-specific GK — state history, geography, culture, and local current affairs — since that's where this paper differs from a pan-India GK section. Cover national current affairs for roughly the last six months too. A 15–20 minute daily newspaper habit, with short notes for quick revision closer to the exam, works better than cramming everything in the final month.

Prelims — Arithmetic

The paper is objective, 100 questions in 60 minutes, so speed matters as much as accuracy here. Percentage, ratio, average, profit & loss, simple/compound interest, and time & work should be your daily practice topics. Aim for 20-25 mixed-topic questions a day pulled from previous year papers, and time yourself — untimed practice won't prepare you for the real pressure.

Prelims — Reasoning

Series completion, coding-decoding, analogy, blood relations, direction sense, and puzzles — these show up repeatedly in state-level exams of this type. Regular practice matters more than depth here; it's a section where speed comes from familiarity, not cleverness.

Mains — Descriptive Paper

This is where the exam gets genuinely tougher than a typical Anganwadi-linked test. It's a 400-mark paper with a 90-minute limit, so practice writing full answers within a strict time frame — not just reading and understanding content. Since the post is directly tied to child welfare work, read up on the ICDS scheme itself, Women & Child Development policies, and West Bengal's social welfare programmes; these aren't side topics, they're core to what examiners expect. And if Bengali proficiency is a stated requirement for the Supervisor post, don't skip practicing the Bengali language section — candidates sometimes underprepare for it assuming it's a formality, which it isn't.

Viva-Voce (Personality Test)

Be ready to talk about the ICDS scheme, your own educational background, and why this specific role interests you — interviewers tend to probe motivation more than textbook knowledge at this stage. Stay current on Women & Child Development news. Mock interviews genuinely help here, mostly because they force you to structure your thoughts out loud rather than just in your head. One full mock test a week alongside your written prep keeps you from losing touch with time management as the exam gets closer.

Should You Apply? A Decision Framework

Not every eligible candidate should jump at this one, and that's worth saying plainly rather than dancing around it.

Apply if: you already hold a bachelor's degree in any stream, you're comfortable with Bengali (spoken and written, since it's generally required), and you're looking for a stable, regular government post rather than a contractual role. If you've got some background or genuine interest in social welfare or child development work, that'll help at the mains and viva stages more than generic exam prep will.

Wait and watch if: you're still finishing your degree and won't have it in hand by the eligibility cutoff — don't apply on a "I'll complete it soon" basis for a post like this. Also hold off if you're purely looking for the fastest possible government job; with a three-stage process and dates not even out yet, this is a longer game than a single-stage recruitment.

Honestly, if you're a fresher with zero exposure to descriptive-answer writing, don't underestimate the Mains stage just because Prelims looks manageable on paper. A lot of candidates clear Prelims comfortably and then struggle with a 400-mark descriptive paper they didn't take seriously enough.

For Cook and Helper posts, the calculus is simpler — Class 8 pass is the bar, and the selection process is expected to be lighter than the Supervisor route (though the notification will confirm exact stages). If you meet the basic qualification and are looking for a Group-D-equivalent government role in this department, there's little downside to applying once the form opens.

When will the WBPSC ICDS Supervisor 2026 notification actually be released?

No fixed date yet — it's still marked "To Be Notified" on official channels. Given the advance intimation is already out, the full notification usually follows within a few weeks to a couple of months, but WBPSC hasn't confirmed a window.

Is the One Time Registration (OTR) the same as the application form?

No — OTR on psc.wb.gov.in is a one-time profile setup, while the actual application for this specific recruitment is a separate form you'll fill after OTR is done. Missing this distinction is a common mistake first-time WBPSC applicants make.

How many total vacancies are expected this year?

Around 16,000 combined across Supervisor, Cook, and Helper posts, though the post-wise breakup isn't out yet. For comparison, the 2019 cycle had 2,954 Supervisor posts alone, so this round is shaping up considerably larger.

Do SC/ST candidates need to pay the application fee?

No — SC/ST candidates from West Bengal and PwBD candidates are exempted from the ₹160 fee, while General category candidates pay the full amount online.

Is Bengali language proficiency compulsory for the Supervisor post?

It's listed as "generally required" for the Supervisor role in the eligibility criteria, which in practice means it matters at the Mains and Viva stages even if it's not a strict rejection criterion at the application stage.

What's the difference in eligibility between Supervisor and Cook & Helper posts?

Supervisor needs a bachelor's degree in any discipline; Cook and Helper only require a Class 8 pass. This gap in eligibility is also why the two groups will likely see very different competition levels per seat.

What does the selection process for ICDS Supervisor look like?

Three stages — an objective Prelims covering General Knowledge, Arithmetic and Reasoning, a 400-mark descriptive Mains paper, and finally a Viva-Voce. It's a longer process than most Anganwadi-linked recruitments in other states.

What salary can a selected ICDS Supervisor expect?

Early estimates suggest a pay range roughly in the ₹27,000–₹30,000/month bracket under the applicable pay structure, though this figure is approximate and the official notification will confirm the exact pay scale.

For candidates who sat out the previous drive hoping for a bigger one this time, that's not great news, but it also means anyone who does clear this cycle is up against a genuinely smaller applicant pool competing for fewer seats, which usually pushes cutoffs up rather than down.

Section Controller sits in an odd spot within Railway recruitment — it's graduate-level, pays at Level 6 like several NTPC posts, but runs its own separate CEN notification instead of getting folded into the general NTPC drive. The job itself involves monitoring and coordinating train movement across a section of track, which is why the selection process leans so heavily on a psychometric-style aptitude test (CBAT) on top of the usual written exam. That combination — CBT plus CBAT — is closer to what ALP or Loco Pilot candidates go through than what typical NTPC Clerk or Station Master aspirants face.

This piece walks through every field in the notification, checks the drop in vacancies against the last cycle and against comparable Railway exams running this season, and then gets into a prep strategy that actually accounts for the CBAT stage most candidates underprepare for.

How the Vacancy Drop Actually Changes Your Odds

Going from 368 seats down to 119 isn't a small correction — it's roughly a 68% cut compared to the CEN 04/2025 cycle. What that likely means in practice: the applicant count probably won't fall anywhere near proportionally, since graduates weighing this exam against NTPC or state PSC options don't necessarily know the seat count shrank before they start preparing. Fewer seats chasing a similar-sized applicant pool usually means a tougher cutoff, not a gentler one, so don't read the smaller number as reduced competition — if anything, treat it as the opposite signal.

Prep Strategy — CBT Alone Isn't the Whole Fight Here

The CBT syllabus itself is fairly standard Railway-exam territory — Averages, Percentages, Time-Speed-Distance, and the usual reasoning topics like Syllogism and Coding-Decoding will look familiar if you've prepped for any other RRB or SSC exam. Reading Comprehension pulling from subjects as varied as Mythology and Environment is a bit unusual, so widen your reading beyond just current affairs and technical topics if that section worries you. What actually separates Section Controller prep from a typical Railway exam is the CBAT. This isn't a subject you can revise — it's a standardised psychometric battery testing things like reaction time, spatial awareness, and decision-making under pressure, the same category of test ALP and Loco Pilot candidates go through. If you've never taken a CBAT-style test before, look up sample CBAT batteries online and get comfortable with the format itself well before your actual test date — showing up cold to an unfamiliar test type is a bigger risk here than being under-revised on percentages.

Should You Apply?

If you're a graduate in any stream who's already comfortable with numerical and reasoning-heavy competitive exams, 119 seats is still worth a shot, especially if your preferred zone — Ahmedabad, Chennai, or Ranchi, going by the seat counts — happens to have a reasonable opening. Honestly, if you already have an NTPC or SSC CGL attempt lined up this season and your prep time is limited, Section Controller's smaller vacancy count means your marginal effort is probably better spent making sure you clear the CBAT comfortably rather than chasing every last CBT mark, since a strong CBT score with a weak CBAT performance still won't get you through.

If numerical reasoning under time pressure genuinely isn't your strength, or you've never encountered a psychometric aptitude test before and have limited time to practice one, this cycle's tighter seat count makes it a riskier bet than the graduate-level NTPC posts running in parallel — where the sheer vacancy volume gives you more room for error.

How many vacancies does this cycle actually have, and how does that compare to last time?

119 posts this cycle, down sharply from 368 in the previous CEN 04/2025 recruitment — a drop of roughly two-thirds, so don't expect this round to be easier just because the syllabus hasn't changed.

Is there really an application fee refund, or is that just for show?

It's real, but conditional — you get ₹400 back (General/OBC/EWS) or the full ₹250 (SC/ST) only if you actually appear for the CBT; skip the exam after paying and the fee is gone for good.

What exactly is the CBAT, and why does it matter so much for this post?

It's a Computer Based Aptitude Test measuring psychometric traits relevant to controlling train movement, and you need a minimum T-Score of 42 in every battery to qualify — a strong CBT score alone won't save you if you fail this stage.

Do all zones have the same number of vacancies?

Not even close — Ahmedabad tops the list with 11 seats, while Jammu-Srinagar (NR) and Mumbai (SCR) show zero seats this cycle despite being listed in the zone breakup.

Can I edit my application after submitting it?

Yes, there's a dedicated correction window from 17 to 26 August 2026, but it comes with a non-refundable ₹250 modification charge on top of whatever you already paid.

What's the minimum qualifying percentage in the CBT for my category?

It varies — 40% for UR and EWS, 30% for OBC and SC, and 25% for ST, with a further 2-mark relaxation for PwBD candidates if there's a shortage of qualified candidates in that group.

How is the final merit list actually calculated — just the CBT score?

No — it's a weighted combination, with your CBT score counting for 70% and your CBAT performance counting for the remaining 30%, so both stages genuinely matter to your final rank.
